```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo    = TRUE,
  message = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE,
  fig.width  = 9,
  fig.height = 6
)

set.seed(1)

# Prevent knitr's inline-r hook from rendering large legacy-slope RQ/CF values
# (e.g. ~1e7 under the pre-fix cumulative volume slope, SPEC 1b) as mangled
# unrendered scientific notation (literal "1.2^{7}" text); does not change any
# computed value, only how numbers print.
options(scipen = 999)

# During an actual render (quarto render / rmarkdown::render()), knitr's working
# directory for THIS chunk is the .qmd's own directory (R/), but that can vary by
# how the render is invoked. Resolve the project root from the file's own known
# location via knitr::current_input() rather than assuming a starting cwd, so this
# works the same whether rendered from the project root, from R/, or via Quarto's
# CLI. Falls back to the current directory when run interactively (chunk-by-chunk),
# where cwd is normally already the project root.
proj_root <- tryCatch({
  doc_path <- knitr::current_input(dir = TRUE)
  if (is.null(doc_path) || !nzchar(doc_path)) stop("not knitting")
  normalizePath(file.path(dirname(doc_path), ".."))
}, error = function(e) normalizePath("."))

knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = proj_root)
getwd()

# ── Global Monte Carlo settings (change here to scale up/down) ──
n_boot <- 10   # bootstrap replicates (increase to ≥ 1000 for publication)
n_mc   <- 20000 # alpha Monte Carlo draws

# Uniform C-PSD bin width for volume fits (µm³), applied identically across every
# matrix and shape (river/sediment/ocean; fragment/fiber/all) — the same convention
# already used for length (bin_um = 5 µm, fixed) and area (bin_um = 500 µm², fixed)
# fits below. Segur et al. (2026) demonstrate the C-PSD method's slope estimate
# should be ~bin-size-independent (RSD < 1.8%) *once the fit window is held fixed*;
# empirical testing here confirms that holds for volume too (RSD ~5-10% across a
# 10x range of bin_um) as long as the window itself isn't also re-optimized per bin
# size — see the volume-lod-bounds chunks below for why the window is fixed via
# length/width-consistent bounds rather than left to auto-detection for volume.
vol_bin_um <- 2e4

# ── Utility functions (sourced from companion scripts in R/) ──
# mp_risk_utils.R – C-PSD fitting, exposure/hazard/risk functions
# cpsd_plotting.R – plot_cpsd_multi(), MP_PALETTE
source(file.path(proj_root, "R", "mp_risk_utils.R"))
source(file.path(proj_root, "R", "cpsd_plotting.R"))
source(file.path(proj_root, "R", "risk_plotting.R"))    # matrix-aware risk plotting helpers

# Hoffman et al. (2026)-motivated sensitivity controls. These are explicit
# assumptions so they can be changed without editing hidden model logic.
slope_structural_sd <- 0.25
hoffman_delta_m     <- 0.10
hoffman_K_m2_s      <- 1e-5
polymer_density_tbl <- polymer_density_lookup()

# ── Additional packages used in plots ──
if (!requireNamespace("ggrepel", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("ggrepel")
if (!requireNamespace("scales",  quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("scales")
library(ggrepel)
library(scales)
```

# 1. Overview

This document presents an **end-to-end, fully probabilistic** environmental risk assessment (ERA) workflow for microplastics in freshwater surface water and sediment from four central California rivers (Carmel, Pajaro, Salinas, and San Lorenzo). The workflow proceeds through five steps:

1. **Raw particle data → power-law slope (α) via C-PSD** — cumulative particle size distribution fitted using the two-step LOD detection algorithm of [Segur et al. (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1186/s43591-026-00205-5).
2. **Monitoring concentrations → probabilistic rescaling** — power-law integration converts measurements from a sampled size range to a target range, propagating slope uncertainty via Monte Carlo ([Coffin et al. 2022](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.scitotenv.2022.155859)).
3. **Environmental Exposure Distribution (EED)** — nonparametric bootstrap of corrected site-level concentrations.
4. **Hazard threshold distribution** — probabilistic species sensitivity distributions (pSSD++) using the [PSSDplusplus R package](https://github.com/ScottCoffin/ToMEx2.0_EcoToxRisk/tree/main/package) and [ToMEx 2.0 toxicity database](https://github.com/ScottCoffin/ToMEx2.0_EcoToxRisk).
5. **Risk characterization** — Monte Carlo pairing of exposure and hazard distributions, expressed as risk quotient (RQ = Exposure/Hazard) and exceedance probability P(RQ > 1).

All custom R functions (`fit_cpsd_segur_r`, `correction_factor`, `bootstrap_eed`, `mc2d_risk`, etc.) live in `R/mp_risk_utils.R` and `R/cpsd_plotting.R` for reuse and eventual integration into **PSSDplusplus**. The Segur et al. (2026) LOD-detection algorithm is implemented directly in `R/mp_risk_utils.R` as pure R.

**Executive summary of Hoffman et al. (2026) revisions.** This revision treats the C-PSD slope convention, transport-induced slope structure, sampling depth, polymer density, and water-sediment PSD coherence as explicit uncertainty sources rather than leaving them implicit. Two related but distinct slope-convention corrections are involved. First (prior revision), the Koelmans/Coffin exposure correction factor and the hazard-side **length**-slope alignment were corrected to integrate the **differential** PSD slope (*a*~psd~ = *a*~cpsd~ − 1) rather than the cumulative C-PSD slope; this is locked by a rendered worked-example assertion in Section 5.1.0 (Koelmans et al. 2020: CF = 8.32 for 30–2000 µm → 1–5000 µm at α = 1.6). Second (this corrective follow-up, SPEC 1b), the hazard-side **volume** and **surface-area** slopes used inside pSSD++'s Food Dilution alignment had been left on the cumulative convention even after the first fix, which inflated the polydisperse mean particle volume and, with it, the Food Dilution risk quotient by orders of magnitude; Section 13.1 corrects this and reports a per-matrix before/after decomposition. This revision also propagates the two-segment (dual-slope) C-PSD diagnostic as a labeled bounding exposure sensitivity rather than a display-only diagnostic (Section 13.3, SPEC 2b). A further corrective follow-up (SPEC 3c) found that the Tissue Translocation attribution in an earlier version of this executive summary was wrong — it called the volume/area-slope fix's effect on Tissue Translocation "essentially unchanged" when the rendered numbers showed otherwise (Section 14.1); that attribution is corrected here. The same follow-up (SPEC 1d) audited the sediment (beach sand) pathway and found its exposure concentration is a per-liter water value mislabeled as particles/kg sediment, with no genuine dry-weight sediment concentration available in the source data; the sediment pathway is therefore retained only as an illustrative/methods demonstration and excluded from the headline risk conclusion (Section 11.3.0/11.4.0/15.3). A further scoped addition (SPEC 1e) reframes sediment as a time-dependent, accumulating compartment in which deposited microplastics continue to fragment in place, so that any single-time-point sediment metric is a lower-bound snapshot rather than a static risk value ([Thuy-Dung, Groenenberg & Koelmans 2026](https://doi.org/10.1186/s43591-026-00210-8); Section 11.5) — this is a framing/sensitivity addition, not a re-introduction of sediment into the headline risk conclusion. A fully quantified, corrected executive summary — including the RQ decomposition that separates the exposure, length-slope, area-slope, and volume-slope contributions — is given in Section 15.3, after all matrices' corrected and legacy sensitivity pipelines have been computed. **No number in this introductory paragraph should be read as the current corrected result; see Section 15.3 for that.**

# 3. Load data

## 3.1 Raw particle-length observations

This data comes from microscopy/FTIR particle measurements (a table of individual particles).

```{r}
# import river particle data (includes plastics and non-plastics)
raw_particles <- readRDS("data_input/Part_dets_comb.rds") |> 
  # filter to only QC-passing particles
  dplyr::filter(!material_class %in% c("mineral", "organic matter"), #filter non-plastic
                acc_analy_conf == "confident", # only use confident spectra
                bad_spectra) %>% #filter out bad spectra
  # extract the first 8-digit block from the ID
  mutate(date_raw = str_extract(Client_ID_MSSupdate, "\\d{8}"), date = ymd(date_raw), # convert YYYYMMDD → Date
         shape = case_when(aspect_ratio >= 3 ~ "fiber", # common definition of fiber - check!
                           aspect_ratio <= 3 ~ "fragment"),
         length_um = max_length_um,
         width_um = min_length_um,
         sample_depth_general = recode(sample_depth_general, "depth" = "subsurface")
  ) |>
  assign_polymer_density(lookup = polymer_density_tbl)

# subset by matrix for downstream analysis
raw_particles_river <- raw_particles |> 
  filter(sample_type == "river water") #river water, ocean water, or beach sand are options

raw_particles_ocean <- raw_particles |> 
  filter(sample_type == "ocean water")

raw_particles_river |> 
  group_by(shape) |> 
  summarize(count = n(),
            mean_length = mean(length_um, na.rm = TRUE),
            min_length = min(length_um, na.rm = TRUE),
            max_length = max(length_um, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd_length = sd(length_um, na.rm = TRUE),
            mean_width = mean(width_um, na.rm = TRUE),
            min_width = min(width_um, na.rm = TRUE),
            max_width = max(width_um, na.rm = TRUE)
            )
```

### 3.1.1 Estimate particle volume

```{r}
# ---- Thickness (height) factor from measured raw data ----
# Kooi et al. (2022) H = r * W, where r is median(W/L). 
ratio_tbl <- raw_particles_river |>
  mutate(
    WL = 1/aspect_ratio,
    # area-derived effective width (rectangle proxy); protects against noisy min_length
    width_eff_um = case_when(
      shape == "fragment" & !is.na(area_um2) & !is.na(length_um) & length_um > 0 &
        !is.na(circularity) & circularity < 0.7 ~ area_um2 / length_um,
      TRUE ~ width_um
    )) |> 
  group_by(shape) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    r_med  = median(WL, na.rm = TRUE),            # central estimate
    r_low  = quantile(WL, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),    # conservative low
    r_high = quantile(WL, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),    # conservative high
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# quick sanity check: ratio table + summary of volumes
ratio_tbl

# ---- Volumes ----
# Ellipsoid (Kooi-compatible): V = (pi/6) * L * W * H  with H = r * W
# => V = (pi/6) * r * L * W^2
# Cylinder assumption for fibers: V = pi * (W/2)^2 * L

raw_particles_river <- raw_particles_river |>
  left_join(ratio_tbl |> dplyr::select(shape, r_med), by = "shape") |>  
  mutate(# thickness in um (assume L/W = H/W)
    height_um = r_med * width_um) |> 

    mutate(# ellipsoid volume in um^3 (primary; Kooi-consistent)
      V_um3  = case_when(shape == "fragment" ~ (pi/6) * length_um * width_um * height_um,
    # fiber cylinder sensitivity in um^3 (only meaningful for fibers)
                        shape == "fiber"    ~ pi * (width_um/2)^2 * length_um,
                        TRUE ~ NA_real_)
                        ) |> 
    # estimate particle mass based on volume and polymer-resolved density; retain
    # the legacy fixed-density case as a labeled sensitivity.
    mutate(
      mass_ug = V_um3 * density_g_cm3,
      mass_ug_fixed_density_1.1 = V_um3 * 1.1
    )

# export CSV of cleaned up raw particles
write.csv(raw_particles_river, "data_output/Part_dets_cleaned.csv", row.names = FALSE)

raw_particles_river |>
  group_by(shape) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    V_um3_median = median(V_um3, na.rm = TRUE),
    V_um3_mean = mean(V_um3, na.rm = TRUE),
    V_um3_sd = sd(V_um3, na.rm = TRUE),
    mass_ug_median = median(mass_ug, na.rm = TRUE),
    mass_ug_mean = mean(mass_ug, na.rm = TRUE),
    mass_ug_sd = sd(mass_ug, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

Hoffman et al. (2026) identify 3-D geometry and density as higher-priority uncertainty sources than fine differences among settling-velocity equations. Particle density is therefore resolved by broad FTIR polymer class where possible (measured polymer class; model-based density lookup; TODO(cite) density table), while the legacy fixed 1.1 g/cm^3 case is retained as a sensitivity column. The buoyant/settling flag is an inferred transport category relative to freshwater or seawater density and is used only in the diagnostic Hoffman sections below.

```{r polymer-density-table}
knitr::kable(
  polymer_density_tbl |>
    dplyr::select(polymer_group, density_g_cm3, source_note),
  caption = "Polymer density lookup used for Hoffman et al. (2026) transport diagnostics. Source details are placeholders until a canonical density table is selected."
)

raw_particles_river |>
  dplyr::count(polymer_density_group, buoyancy_freshwater, sort = TRUE) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "River particle density groups and freshwater buoyancy flags")
```

## 3.2 Monitoring concentration observations (site replicates)

Here we load monitoring replicate concentrations (particles/L) that were *reported for limited size ranges* (e.g., 300–5000 µm typical of net tows).

```{r}
monitoring <- readRDS("data_input/Part_dets_summ.rds") |> 
  filter(sample_type == "river water",
         material_simple == "plastic",
         sample_or_blank == "sample"
  ) %>% 
  mutate(# extract the first 8-digit block from the ID
    date_raw = str_extract(Client_ID_MSSupdate, "\\d{8}"),  
    # convert YYYYMMDD → Date
    date = ymd(date_raw),    
    # correct the specific sample date
    date = case_when(
      Client_ID_MSSupdate == "SRR20250303SS" ~ ymd("20250303"),
      TRUE ~ date
    ),
    sample_dets = case_when(Client_ID_MSSupdate %in% c("CRR20231207SS", "CRR20231207SD") ~ "lagoon",
                            Client_ID_MSSupdate %in% c("SRR20231207SS", "SRR20231207SD") ~ "lagoon"),
    # recode depth to subsurface
    sample_depth_general = recode(sample_depth_general,
                                  "depth" = "subsurface"),
    sample_depth_general = factor(
      sample_depth_general,
      levels = c("subsurface", "surface")
    ) 
  ) %>%
  rename(river = sample_location,
         C_measured_pL = extrap_conc_PPL) |> 
          # should adjust based on power law LLOD determined below
  mutate(Lmin_measured_um = 50, 
         Lmax_measured_um = 500,
         sample_id = Client_ID_MSSupdate)

head(monitoring)
```


# 4. Step 1 — Derive power-law alpha via C-PSD (binned cumulative PSD)

## 4.1 C-PSD fitting — Segur et al. (2026)

The C-PSD (cumulative particle size distribution) method fits N(≥L) vs L on a log-log scale
using **binned** count data, removing the bin-width bias inherent in the classic BN-PSD approach
([Segur et al. 2026](https://doi.org/10.1186/s43591-026-00205-5)). The algorithm is implemented
in pure R in `R/mp_risk_utils.R` as `fit_cpsd_segur_r()`.

**Two-step LOD detection algorithm:**

1. Bin particle measurements; compute BN-PSD and C-PSD.
2. Global OLS on all bins → normalised residuals; retain bins with *positive* residuals at or
   above the BN-PSD peak (Low_size ≥ L_max of the BN-PSD).
3. Exhaustively test all contiguous sub-windows ≥ 3 bins; accept windows with R² ≥ 0.90.
4. Select the **longest** accepted window (ties broken by R²) as the fitting range.
5. OLS on log₁₀ N(≥L) ~ log₁₀ L_low; BN-PSD slope a = a_cpsd − 1.

## 4.2 Fit C-PSD to the raw particle data

### 4.2.1 Particle Length

```{r cpsd-fits-by-shape}
# Pooled C-PSD fits across all river locations, bin_um = 5 µm
cpsd_fits_river_length <- fit_cpsd_by_shape(
  raw_particles_river, value_col = "length_um",
  config = list(
    fragment = list(bin_um = 5, fit_range_um = c(NA_real_, NA_real_)),
    fiber    = list(bin_um = 5, fit_range_um = c(NA_real_, NA_real_)),
    all      = list(bin_um = 5, fit_range_um = c(NA_real_, NA_real_))
  )
)
cpsd_fit_frag  <- cpsd_fits_river_length$fragment
cpsd_fit_fiber <- cpsd_fits_river_length$fiber
cpsd_fit_all   <- cpsd_fits_river_length$all
```

The Segur et al. (2026) algorithm fitted power-law slopes of α_CPSD = `r round(cpsd_fit_frag$a_cpsd, 2)` ± `r round(cpsd_fit_frag$se_a_cpsd, 2)` for fragments (LOD `r round(cpsd_fit_frag$lower_lod_used_um)` – `r round(cpsd_fit_frag$upper_lod_um)` µm), α_CPSD = `r round(cpsd_fit_fiber$a_cpsd, 2)` ± `r round(cpsd_fit_fiber$se_a_cpsd, 2)` for fibers (LOD `r round(cpsd_fit_fiber$lower_lod_used_um)` – `r round(cpsd_fit_fiber$upper_lod_um)` µm), and α_CPSD = `r round(cpsd_fit_all$a_cpsd, 2)` ± `r round(cpsd_fit_all$se_a_cpsd, 2)` for all particles pooled (LOD `r round(cpsd_fit_all$lower_lod_used_um)` – `r round(cpsd_fit_all$upper_lod_um)` µm, R² = `r round(cpsd_fit_all$r2, 3)`). The corresponding differential BN-PSD slopes (a = α_CPSD − 1) are `r round(cpsd_fit_frag$a_psd, 2)` (fragment), `r round(cpsd_fit_fiber$a_psd, 2)` (fiber), and `r round(cpsd_fit_all$a_psd, 2)` (all). For comparison, [Segur et al. (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1186/s43591-026-00205-5) report a mean BN-PSD slope of −2.66 ± 0.68 for fragments across ocean and atmosphere samples.

```{r cpsd-fits-by-location}
# Per-location fits (Carmel, Pajaro, Salinas, San Lorenzo) — all particles pooled by site
locations <- sort(unique(raw_particles_river$sample_location))

cpsd_fits_by_loc <- lapply(setNames(locations, locations), function(loc) {
  dat <- raw_particles_river |> dplyr::filter(sample_location == loc) |> dplyr::pull(length_um)
  c(fit_cpsd_segur_r(dat, bin_um = 5), list(shape = loc))
})

# Summary table: slope and LOD window by location
loc_summary <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(cpsd_fits_by_loc), function(loc) {
  fo <- cpsd_fits_by_loc[[loc]]
  tibble::tibble(
    location     = loc,
    n_particles  = sum(raw_particles_river$sample_location == loc),
    a_cpsd       = round(fo$a_cpsd,   3),
    se_a_cpsd    = round(fo$se_a_cpsd, 3),
    a_psd        = round(fo$a_psd,    3),
    lod_low_um   = round(fo$lower_lod_used_um, 0),
    lod_high_um  = round(fo$upper_lod_um,       0),
    r2           = round(fo$r2,       3),
    n_bins       = fo$n_bins,
    fit_mode     = fo$fit_mode
  )
}))

knitr::kable(loc_summary, caption = "C-PSD length fits by river location (Segur 2026 algorithm)")
```

```{r cpsd-location-slope-plot}
cpsd_location_slope_plot <- loc_summary |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(x = location, y = a_psd)) +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = -2.66, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50", linewidth = 0.7) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 4, color = "#56B4E9") +
  ggplot2::geom_errorbar(
    ggplot2::aes(ymin = a_psd - se_a_cpsd, ymax = a_psd + se_a_cpsd),
    width = 0.2, color = "#56B4E9", linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  ggplot2::annotate("text", x = Inf, y = -2.66,
                    label = "Segur 2026 fragment mean (−2.66)",
                    size = 3.2, hjust = 1.05, vjust = -0.5, color = "gray40") +
  ggplot2::coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-4, -1)) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = seq(-4, -1, by = 0.5),
    labels = function(x) formatC(x, digits = 1, format = "f")
  ) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x        = "River location",
    y        = expression(italic(a)[psd] ~ "=" ~ italic(a)[cpsd] - 1),
    title    = "Power-law slope by river location",
    subtitle = expression("Error bars = ±1 SE  |  Dashed = Segur 2026 reference")
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 20) +
  ggplot2::theme(panel.border = ggplot2::element_rect(color = "gray85", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.4))

ggsave(cpsd_location_slope_plot, filename = "figures/cpsd_location_slope_plot.png", width = 9, height = 6, dpi = 300)
```

#### 4.2.1.2 Literature comparison of power-law size distribution slopes

The differential BN-PSD slope *a*~psd~ = *a*~cpsd~ − 1 (equivalent to the negative power-law exponent α in Kooi et al. 2021) characterizes how steeply particle abundance declines with increasing size. Steeper (more negative) *a*~psd~ values indicate that small particles dominate the count distribution far more strongly than large ones. Comparing this slope across studies and analytical methods provides a critical cross-check on data quality and reveals how sampling methodology shapes the apparent size distribution.

**Notation reconciliation.** Different publications use different sign conventions. Zhao et al. (2026) and Kooi et al. (2021) report the *positive* exponent α from the probability density function *f*(*L*) ∝ *L*^−α^; their α corresponds directly to |*a*~psd~| in our Segur notation. Wang et al. (2026) follow the same positive-α convention. Segur et al. (2026) report the negative C-PSD slope *a*~cpsd~, from which *a*~psd~ = *a*~cpsd~ − 1.

```{r alpha-literature-comparison-table, echo=FALSE}
# Kooi et al. (2021) length-slope (alpha) reference values, as embedded in
# PSSDplusplus::param_default_values (alpha.freshwater, alpha.marine) — the same
# source used elsewhere in this document for surface-area/volume/mass defaults.
kooi_alpha_freshwater <- PSSDplusplus::param_default_values$alpha.freshwater
kooi_alpha_marine     <- PSSDplusplus::param_default_values$alpha.marine

lit_alpha_df <- data.frame(
  Source = c(
    paste0("This study — fragments (µFTIR, Segur LOD, ", round(cpsd_fit_frag$lower_lod_used_um), "–", round(cpsd_fit_frag$upper_lod_um), " µm)"),
    paste0("This study — fibers (µFTIR, Segur LOD, ", round(cpsd_fit_fiber$lower_lod_used_um), "–", round(cpsd_fit_fiber$upper_lod_um), " µm)"),
    paste0("This study — all shapes (µFTIR, Segur LOD, ", round(cpsd_fit_all$lower_lod_used_um), "–", round(cpsd_fit_all$upper_lod_um), " µm)"),
    "Wang et al. 2026 — Rhine/Meuse combined suspended solids (µFTIR)",
    "Wang et al. 2026 — Rhine Lobith samples (µFTIR, mean)",
    "Wang et al. 2026 — Meuse Eijsden samples (µFTIR, mean)",
    "Segur et al. 2026 — ocean reference (C-PSD)",
    "Segur et al. 2026 — atmosphere reference (C-PSD)",
    "Zhao et al. 2026 — global surface water meta-analysis (45 studies)",
    "Zhao et al. 2026 — mesh-adjusted global surface water",
    "Kooi et al. 2021 — freshwater surface water default",
    "Kooi et al. 2021 — marine surface water default"
  ),
  Convention = c(
    rep("C-PSD a_cpsd (negative)", 3),
    rep("BN-PSD +α (positive)", 3),
    rep("C-PSD a_cpsd (negative)", 2),
    rep("BN-PSD +α (positive)", 4)
  ),
  Reported_alpha = c(
    round(cpsd_fit_frag$a_cpsd, 3),
    round(cpsd_fit_fiber$a_cpsd, 3),
    round(cpsd_fit_all$a_cpsd, 3),
    3.65, 3.89, 3.19,
    -1.66, -1.55,
    1.50, 1.53, kooi_alpha_freshwater, kooi_alpha_marine
  ),
  Equivalent_a_psd = c(
    round(cpsd_fit_frag$a_cpsd - 1, 3),
    round(cpsd_fit_fiber$a_cpsd - 1, 3),
    round(cpsd_fit_all$a_cpsd - 1, 3),
    -3.65, -3.89, -3.19,
    -2.66, -2.55,
    -1.50, -1.53, -kooi_alpha_freshwater, -kooi_alpha_marine
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)
colnames(lit_alpha_df) <- c("Source", "Convention", "Reported value", "Equivalent a_psd")
knitr::kable(lit_alpha_df,
  caption = "Power-law size distribution slopes: this study vs. recent literature. All values converted to the BN-PSD differential slope a_psd for comparability.",
  digits = 3, align = "llrr"
)
```

**Key finding — consistency with µFTIR studies, divergence from net-trawl surveys.** Our fragment *a*~psd~ (`r round(cpsd_fit_frag$a_cpsd - 1, 2)`) and all-shape *a*~psd~ (`r round(cpsd_fit_all$a_cpsd - 1, 2)`) are within the range reported by Wang et al. (2026) for Dutch river suspended solids measured by µFTIR (−3.19 to −3.89, mean combined −3.65, SD 0.21). This agreement is not surprising: both datasets use particle-by-particle µFTIR counting on filtered samples. In contrast, our values are substantially steeper than the global surface water meta-analysis compiled by Zhao et al. (2026; mean α = 1.50, equivalent *a*~psd~ = −1.50, SD 0.53) and the freshwater/marine surface-water defaults reported by Kooi et al. (2021; α = `r round(kooi_alpha_freshwater, 2)` freshwater, `r round(kooi_alpha_marine, 2)` marine). The Segur et al. (2026) reference slopes (ocean −1.66, atmosphere −1.55 in C-PSD notation, equivalent *a*~psd~ ≈ −2.66 and −2.55) are intermediate.

The divergence from the Zhao/Kooi global averages likely reflects three interacting factors: (1) **analytical resolution** — µFTIR counting captures particles approaching ~20 µm, whereas most studies in the Zhao meta-analysis used net trawls or pump samples with mesh sizes ≥ 300 µm, systematically missing the numerically dominant small-particle fraction and producing an apparent shallower slope; (2) **size range of fit** — our Segur LOD algorithm fits the C-PSD over a restricted window (~100–330 µm for fragments) within which the distribution is inherently steeper than a global fit spanning three orders of magnitude; (3) **environmental context** — California coastal rivers may differ from open-ocean or mixed-environment global compilations.

**Fiber vs. fragment.** Fibers exhibit a notably shallower slope (*a*~psd~ = `r round(cpsd_fit_fiber$a_cpsd - 1, 2)`) than fragments (*a*~psd~ = `r round(cpsd_fit_frag$a_cpsd - 1, 2)`). This is consistent with Zhao et al. (2026), who found that fibers have dramatically lower mesh capture efficiency (0.70% at 330 µm mesh; 37.6% at 20 µm mesh across a 10–5000 µm size range) compared to fragments (7.9% at 330 µm). While our µFTIR pump-and-filter approach avoids the coarsest mesh bias, filter capture of fine fibers (whose short axis — diameter ≤ 10 µm — can pass through a nominal 50 µm pore) may still be lower than for equidimensional fragments. A shallower measured fiber slope would result if fine fibers are under-retained, making observed fiber concentrations a minimum estimate. Users comparing fiber-specific concentrations across studies should be aware of this potential systematic bias.

**Implications for data correction.** Three recently published correction methodologies were evaluated for applicability to this workflow:

1. *Zhao et al. (2026) — Mesh selectivity correction*: This physically-based model corrects for particle loss during mesh-based net trawling or pump filtration. It is **not applied here** because (a) our particle data derive from µFTIR analysis of membrane-filtered samples where the Segur LOD algorithm explicitly identifies and corrects for the analytical lower detection limit; (b) the Zhao model is calibrated for net trawls (mesh aperture as the primary parameter) rather than membrane filtration; and (c) our `correction_factor()` function already accounts for size-range sampling bias through power-law integration, which accomplishes the same conceptual goal. Applying the Zhao correction on top of the existing CF would risk double-counting the lower-size adjustment.

2. *Wang et al. (2026) — µFTIR objective and sieve effects*: Wang et al. demonstrated that the 4× µFTIR objective captures only 3 ± 3% of particles relative to the 25× objective (predominantly because the 4× misses sub-50 µm particles). The sieve mesh size (20 µm vs. 5 µm) had minimal effect on size distribution or polymer composition. The present dataset was collected with an approximately 4× objective at **25 µm pixel size**, giving a detection floor of ~50 µm. Critically, this floor is already reflected in `L_meas_min = 50 µm`, and the power-law CF extrapolates particle counts from this floor to 1 µm. The Wang et al. ×33 factor therefore does **not** apply here — it would double-count the sub-50 µm extrapolation already performed by the CF. A detailed analysis of this intersection and the residual uncertainty in the 50–100 µm marginal detection zone is presented in Section 10.2.

3. *Chen et al. (2026) — Count-to-mass conversion*: Chen et al. developed a conditional fragmentation distribution (CFD, Weibull-based) model for converting particle counts to mass, outperforming the simple power-law (CPD) approach. This methodology is **not applicable** to the present count-based risk assessment workflow (exposure expressed as particles/L); it would be relevant only if mass-based exposure concentrations were required for comparison with mass-normalized ecotoxicological thresholds.

**Summary.** The Segur et al. (2026) LOD detection and power-law correction workflow remains methodologically consistent for central California riverine monitoring data, and the measured slopes are coherent with other µFTIR-based riverine studies. However, Hoffman et al. (2026) adds a separate unresolved uncertainty: transport-induced PSD distortion can affect the validity of a single-power-law extrapolation and can differ by depth, shape, and polymer buoyancy. The analysis therefore keeps the mesh-selectivity and Wang et al. correction exclusions unchanged, but adds Hoffman sensitivity analyses for slope convention, structural slope uncertainty, depth stratification, density/buoyancy, and water-sediment coherence. The current interpretation is that absolute concentrations are more uncertain than previously stated; the Food Dilution vs. Tissue Translocation ranking is likely robust but is no longer treated as immune to PSD-structure effects.

### Volume C-PSD Fitting

`volume_particle()` (sourced from `R/mp_risk_utils.R`) converts length LODs to volume LODs
using the same shape-dependent geometry as the particle volume calculation in section 3.1.1.

```{r volume-lod-bounds}
# volume_lod_bounds() (sourced from R/mp_risk_utils.R) converts each shape's length-LOD
# window into a volume-LOD window using the *measured* width/length ratio (r_med) for
# that shape, rather than assuming an isotropic (L=W=H) particle — so the fit range stays
# consistent with the actual length/width measurements. The "all" (pooled shapes) range is
# the union of the fragment and fiber ranges.
r_med_frag_river  <- ratio_tbl$r_med[ratio_tbl$shape == "fragment"]
r_med_fiber_river <- ratio_tbl$r_med[ratio_tbl$shape == "fiber"]
vlb_river <- volume_lod_bounds(cpsd_fit_frag, cpsd_fit_fiber, r_med_frag_river, r_med_fiber_river)
cat("Fragment volume LOD: [", signif(vlb_river$fragment[1], 2), ",", signif(vlb_river$fragment[2], 2), "] µm³\n")
cat("Fiber    volume LOD: [", signif(vlb_river$fiber[1],    2), ",", signif(vlb_river$fiber[2],    2), "] µm³\n")
cat("All      volume LOD: [", signif(vlb_river$all[1],      2), ",", signif(vlb_river$all[2],      2), "] µm³\n")
```

```{r cpsd-per-river-fits, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, cache=FALSE}
# Fit C-PSD per river × shape for all three metrics.
# Uses tryCatch to handle sparse data combinations gracefully.
safe_cpsd <- function(data, ...) {
  if (length(data) < 10) return(list(valid = FALSE))
  tryCatch(
    c(fit_cpsd_segur_r(data, ...), list(valid = TRUE)),
    error = function(e) list(valid = FALSE)
  )
}

    all      = safe_cpsd(sub |> dplyr::pull(length_um), bin_um = 5)

    fiber    = safe_cpsd(sub |> dplyr::filter(shape == "fiber")    |> dplyr::pull(V_um3),

# Helper: extract LOD bounds from a fit object
.lod_bounds <- function(fo) {
  lod_lo <- if (!is.null(fo$lower_lod_used_um) && is.finite(fo$lower_lod_used_um))
               fo$lower_lod_used_um else fo$lower_lod_um
  list(lo = lod_lo, hi = fo$upper_lod_um)
}

# Extract predicted lines + 95% CI ribbon within each fit's valid LOD window
extract_fit_lines <- function(fits_by_loc, metric_name) {
  dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(fits_by_loc), function(loc) {
    dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(fits_by_loc[[loc]]), function(shp) {
      fo <- fits_by_loc[[loc]][[shp]]
      if (!isTRUE(fo$valid) || is.null(fo$fit)) return(NULL)
      b <- .lod_bounds(fo)
      if (!is.finite(b$lo) || !is.finite(b$hi) || b$lo >= b$hi) return(NULL)
      grid <- tibble::tibble(L_low = seq(b$lo, b$hi, length.out = 80))
      pred <- tryCatch(predict(fo$fit, newdata = grid, se.fit = TRUE), error = function(e) NULL)
      if (is.null(pred)) return(NULL)
      tibble::tibble(metric = metric_name, shape = shp, location = loc,
                     L_low    = grid$L_low,
                     logN_fit = pred$fit,
                     logN_lo  = pred$fit - 1.96 * pred$se.fit,
                     logN_hi  = pred$fit + 1.96 * pred$se.fit)
    }))
  }))
}

# Extract raw binned data points with an in_lod flag for opacity mapping
extract_fit_points <- function(fits_by_loc, metric_name) {
  dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(fits_by_loc), function(loc) {
    dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(fits_by_loc[[loc]]), function(shp) {
      fo <- fits_by_loc[[loc]][[shp]]
      if (!isTRUE(fo$valid) || is.null(fo$bins)) return(NULL)
      b <- .lod_bounds(fo)
      fo$bins |>
        dplyr::arrange(L_low) |>
        dplyr::mutate(
          N_ge   = rev(cumsum(rev(n))),
          in_lod = is.finite(b$lo) & is.finite(b$hi) & L_low >= b$lo & L_high <= b$hi
        ) |>
        dplyr::filter(L_low > 0, N_ge > 0) |>
        dplyr::transmute(metric = metric_name, shape = shp, location = loc,
                         L_low, logN = log10(N_ge), in_lod)
    }))
  }))
}

# River location colour palette (defined once, reused in both chunks)
loc_palette <- c(
  "Carmel"      = "#E69F00",
  "Pajaro"      = "#56B4E9",
  "Salinas"     = "#009E73",
  "San Lorenzo" = "#CC79A7"
)

factor_levels <- list(
  metric = c("Length (µm)", "Surface Area (µm²)", "Volume (µm³)"),
  shape  = c("fragment", "fiber", "all"),
  slabel = c("Fragment",  "Fiber",  "All shapes")
)

cpsd_loc_lines <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  extract_fit_lines(cpsd_loc_shape_length, "Length (µm)"),
  extract_fit_lines(cpsd_loc_shape_area,   "Surface Area (µm²)"),
  extract_fit_lines(cpsd_loc_shape_vol,    "Volume (µm³)")
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    metric   = factor(metric, levels = factor_levels$metric),
    shape    = factor(shape,  levels = factor_levels$shape, labels = factor_levels$slabel),
    location = factor(location, levels = locations)
  ) |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(logN_fit))

cpsd_loc_points <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  extract_fit_points(cpsd_loc_shape_length, "Length (µm)"),
  extract_fit_points(cpsd_loc_shape_area,   "Surface Area (µm²)"),
  extract_fit_points(cpsd_loc_shape_vol,    "Volume (µm³)")
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    metric   = factor(metric, levels = factor_levels$metric),
    shape    = factor(shape,  levels = factor_levels$shape, labels = factor_levels$slabel),
    location = factor(location, levels = locations)
  ) |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(logN))
```

### 4.2.5 Per-river power-law slopes across size metrics

The per-location C-PSD fits from Section 4.2.4 yield a BN-PSD slope *a*~psd~ for each combination of river location and size metric (length, surface area, volume). Comparing these slopes across metrics shows how the shape of the size distribution changes with the geometric measure used, and whether location-to-location variation is consistent across metrics.

```{r cpsd-slopes-all-metrics, fig.width=10, fig.height=4.5}
# Extract per-location a_psd for surface area and volume from the per-river fits
extract_loc_slopes <- function(fits_by_loc, metric_name) {
  dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(fits_by_loc), function(loc) {
    fo <- fits_by_loc[[loc]][["all"]]
    if (!isTRUE(fo$valid) || is.null(fo$fit)) return(NULL)
    tibble::tibble(location = loc, a_psd = fo$a_psd, se_a_cpsd = fo$se_a_cpsd, metric = metric_name)
  }))
}

loc_slopes_all <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  dplyr::transmute(loc_summary, location, a_psd, se_a_cpsd, metric = "Length (µm)"),
  extract_loc_slopes(cpsd_loc_shape_area, "Surface Area (µm²)"),
  extract_loc_slopes(cpsd_loc_shape_vol,  "Volume (µm³)")
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    metric   = factor(metric, levels = c("Length (µm)", "Surface Area (µm²)", "Volume (µm³)")),
    location = factor(location, levels = locations)
  )

# Reference slopes (Segur 2026 ocean mean, length metric)
ref_slopes <- data.frame(
  metric    = factor("Length (µm)", levels = levels(loc_slopes_all$metric)),
  ref_slope = -2.66,
  ref_label = "Segur 2026\nfragment mean"
)

cpsd_slopes_all_metrics_plot <- ggplot2::ggplot(loc_slopes_all,
    ggplot2::aes(x = location, y = a_psd, color = location)) +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(
    data = ref_slopes,
    ggplot2::aes(yintercept = ref_slope),
    linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50", linewidth = 0.7, inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 4) +
  ggplot2::geom_errorbar(
    ggplot2::aes(ymin = a_psd - se_a_cpsd, ymax = a_psd + se_a_cpsd),
    width = 0.2, linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ metric, nrow = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  ggplot2::scale_color_manual(values = loc_palette, guide = "none") +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x        = "River location",
    y        = expression(italic(a)[psd]),
    title    = "BN-PSD slope by river location and size metric",
    subtitle = "Error bars = ±1 SE  |  Dashed = Segur 2026 fragment reference (length only)"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 20) +
  ggplot2::theme(
    panel.border = ggplot2::element_rect(color = "gray85", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.4),
    strip.text   = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.text.x = ggplot2::element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

ggsave(cpsd_slopes_all_metrics_plot, filename = "figures/cpsd_slopes_all_metrics_plot.png", width = 11, height = 7, dpi = 300)
cpsd_slopes_all_metrics_plot
```

Following the probabilistic rescaling approach (e.g., Coffin et al. 2022), treat the **differential** PSD slope as uncertain and represent it by a truncated normal distribution. The Segur C-PSD fit estimates *a*~cpsd~ for N(≥L); the Koelmans et al. (2020), Kooi et al. (2021), and Coffin et al. (2022) correction-factor equation integrates dN/dL = k·L^*a*, so the slope passed to `correction_factor()` is *a*~psd~ = *a*~cpsd~ − 1. Hoffman et al. (2026) adds a model-based structural uncertainty concern: transport can produce apparent dual-slope PSDs whose exponents differ by about two, so `slope_structural_sd` = `r slope_structural_sd` is added as an explicit assumption beyond the fit SE.

```{r alpha-distribution}
# Local seed (guardrail: order-independent of any later relocation/reordering of
# other sections relative to this one -- see docs/CHANGELOG_hoffman_revisions.md).
set.seed(8001)
alpha_fit_only <- alpha_dist(mu = cpsd_fit_all$a_psd, sd = cpsd_fit_all$se_a_psd, n = n_mc, structural_sd = 0)
alpha    <- alpha_dist(mu = cpsd_fit_all$a_psd, sd = cpsd_fit_all$se_a_psd, n = n_mc, structural_sd = slope_structural_sd)
alpha_mu <- mean(alpha)
alpha_se <- sd(alpha)
summary(alpha)
```

The resulting differential slope distribution has mean `r round(alpha_mu, 3)` and SD `r round(alpha_se, 3)`. Fit-only draws are retained as `alpha_fit_only` so the Hoffman structural-uncertainty sensitivity can report before/after effects without changing the fitted C-PSD itself.

# 5. Step 2 — Rescale measured concentrations to a common size range

## 5.1 Power-law integration for rescaling factors

If the differential PSD follows dN/dL = k·L^a, the concentration in [L₁, L₂] is
proportional to k/(a+1)·(L₂^(a+1) − L₁^(a+1)) (a ≠ −1). The rescaling correction factor is:

CF = N(L_target_min, L_target_max) / N(L_meas_min, L_meas_max)

`correction_factor()` is sourced from `R/mp_risk_utils.R` ([Coffin et al. 2022](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.scitotenv.2022.155859)).
The measured size range is bias-corrected using the C-PSD LOD window from `cpsd_fit_all`.

### 5.1.0 Convention guard (SPEC 1c): Koelmans et al. (2020) worked example

Because the correction-factor convention now drives both the exposure rescaling and (after SPEC 1b, below) the hazard-side ERM alignment, it is guarded here by a visible, rendered worked-example assertion rather than relying only on an unrendered test file. [Koelmans et al. (2020)](https://edepot.wur.nl/533506) report that rescaling a measured 30–2000 µm range to a 1–5000 µm target range at a differential slope of α = 1.6 gives CF = 8.32 (e.g., 100 particles/L → 832 particles/L). The Koelmans α is expressed as a positive-magnitude differential (PDF) slope, so it is passed to `correction_factor()` as `a = -1.6` with `slope_convention = "differential"`. This guard enforces the differential convention used throughout the report; if the convention regresses (e.g., a cumulative slope is passed where a differential slope is expected), the assertion below fails loudly and the render stops.

```{r koelmans-convention-check}
cf_check <- correction_factor(
  a = -1.6, L_meas_min = 30, L_meas_max = 2000,
  L_tar_min = 1, L_tar_max = 5000, slope_convention = "differential"
)
stopifnot(abs(cf_check - 8.32) < 0.05)   # Koelmans et al. (2020) worked example

# Companion guard: lock the C-PSD cumulative-to-differential relationship
# (a_psd = a_cpsd - 1) on a real fit object used throughout this report.
stopifnot(abs((cpsd_fit_all$a_psd) - (cpsd_fit_all$a_cpsd - 1)) < 1e-6)

cat(sprintf(
  "Convention check passed: CF(30-2000 um -> 1-5000 um, alpha=1.6) = %.3f (Koelmans et al. 2020 reference: 8.32)\n",
  cf_check
))
```

The equivalent check is also encoded as an automated `testthat` guard in `tests/testthat/test-correction_factor.R`, so the convention is protected both in interactive/rendered use and in CI-style test runs.

```{r rescaling-cf}
# correct_and_bootstrap_eed() (sourced from R/mp_risk_utils.R) bundles the LOD bias
# correction, the power-law correction_factor() rescale, the Monte Carlo corrected-
# concentration draws, and the EED bootstrap into one shared step used identically
# across river/sediment/ocean.
set.seed(9101)
river_corr <- correct_and_bootstrap_eed(
  monitoring  = monitoring,
  conc_col    = "C_measured_pL",
  cpsd_fit    = cpsd_fit_all,
  alpha_draws = alpha,
  L_tar_min   = 1,
  L_tar_max   = 5000,
  n_draws     = 3000,
  n_boot      = n_boot,
  probs       = c(0.5, 0.95),
  slope_convention = "differential"
)
monitoring         <- river_corr$monitoring
L_meas_min_use     <- river_corr$L_meas_min_use
L_meas_max_use     <- river_corr$L_meas_max_use
combined_cf        <- river_corr$combined_cf
C_corrected_draws  <- river_corr$C_corrected_draws
C_sample_median    <- river_corr$C_sample_median
eed_boot           <- river_corr$eed_boot

quantile(combined_cf, c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95))

```

The differential-slope convention (length, area, volume, mass) is the current basis; Appendix A quantifies the effect of each prior convention error.

The median rescaling factor is `r round(median(combined_cf), 2)` (90% CI: `r round(quantile(combined_cf, 0.05), 2)` – `r round(quantile(combined_cf, 0.95), 2)`), applied to convert concentrations measured over `r round(L_meas_min_use)` – `r round(L_meas_max_use)` µm to the target range of 1 – 5000 µm. This is a model-based count correction: `correction_factor()` integrates the differential PSD exponent directly as `L^(a + 1)`, and no internal conversion is applied when `slope_convention = "differential"`.

## 5.2 Optional additional bias terms as probability distributions

Coffin et al. (2022) describe two additional multiplicative correction terms that can be composed with the power-law rescaling CF:

- **Fiber correction factor ($\text{CF}_\text{fiber}$):** Accounts for systematic fiber under-retention during *mesh-based* sampling (net trawls, pump filtration with woven sieves). In those contexts, the slender geometry of fibers allows them to pass through mesh apertures lengthwise, producing under-counts that are proportional to mesh size (Zhao et al. 2026). A log-normal distribution is appropriate because the factor is right-skewed and strictly positive.
- **Plastic proportion factor ($p_\text{plastic}$):** The fraction of detected particles confirmed as plastic by spectroscopy. A Beta($\alpha$, $\beta$) distribution is appropriate because the factor is bounded to [0, 1].

**Assessment for this dataset.** A fiber correction factor is **not applied here** for two reasons:

1. *Sampling method:* The present monitoring data are from µFTIR analysis of membrane-filtered whole-water grab samples (pump collection), not mesh net trawls. Zhao et al. (2026) demonstrate that the dramatic fiber under-capture they quantify (0.7% efficiency at 330 µm mesh) arises specifically from the geometric interaction of elongated particles with woven mesh apertures. Membrane pore filtration retains particles primarily by size, so this mechanism does not apply.
2. *Power-law extrapolation already corrects for sub-LOD fibers:* The `correction_factor()` function in Step 2 uses the fitted power-law slope to integrate particle counts from the measured size range (50–500 µm) to the target range (1–5000 µm). This extrapolation already accounts for undetected small fibers in a self-consistent way. Applying an additional fiber CF on top would double-count this adjustment.

The fiber slope ($a_\text{psd}$ = `r round(cpsd_fit_fiber$a_cpsd - 1, 2)`) is shallower than the fragment slope (`r round(cpsd_fit_frag$a_cpsd - 1, 2)`), which may reflect residual under-retention of the finest fibers through nominal 50 µm filter pores, but this cannot be corrected without fiber-specific filter efficiency data. See Section 4.2.1.2 for the literature comparison.

```{r combined-cf}
# combined_cf was already computed above (Section 5.1, via correct_and_bootstrap_eed());
# the optional fiber/plastic-proportion factors described above are not multiplied in
# (neither is applicable to this µFTIR membrane-filter dataset -- see rationale above).
quantile(combined_cf, c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95))
```

## 5.3 Apply probabilistic correction to monitoring data

We treat each monitoring sample's corrected concentration as:

`C_corrected = C_measured * combined_cf_draw`, with `combined_cf_draw` sampled in Monte Carlo.

This yields a **distribution per monitoring sample**, and a pooled exposure distribution across samples.

```{r}
# For simplicity, assume the same CF distribution applies to each sample.
# If CF depends on site/method/shape, build CF distributions per strata and apply accordingly.
# C_corrected_draws was already computed above (Section 5.1, via correct_and_bootstrap_eed()).

C_corrected_draws |>
  summarise(p05 = quantile(C_corrected, 0.05),
            p50 = quantile(C_corrected, 0.50),
            p95 = quantile(C_corrected, 0.95))
```

# 6. Step 3 — Environmental Exposure Distribution (EED) via empirical bootstrap

Because environmental monitoring data are typically sparse and highly skewed, a **nonparametric bootstrap** is often a strong default:

-   Resample (with replacement) the corrected sample-level concentrations.
-   Compute the empirical CDF and desired percentiles per bootstrap replicate.
-   This avoids heavy reliance on a parametric distribution family selection for EEDs.

```{r eed-bootstrap}
# Collapse each sample to its median corrected concentration, then bootstrap across samples.
# This isolates site-level variability from correction-factor uncertainty (handled in MC2D below).
# C_sample_median / eed_boot were already computed above (Section 5.1, via
# correct_and_bootstrap_eed(), which internally calls bootstrap_eed()).
summary(eed_boot)
```

The median EED 50th percentile across `r n_boot` bootstrap replicates is `r round(median(eed_boot$q50), 2)` particles/L (90th percentile bootstrap: `r round(median(eed_boot$q95), 2)` particles/L).

```{r eed-bootstrap-plot}
eed_bootstrap_plot <- plot_eed_bootstrap(eed_boot, n_boot, "River water")

ggsave(eed_bootstrap_plot, filename = "figures/eed_bootstrap_plot.png", width = 9, height = 6, dpi = 300)
eed_bootstrap_plot
```

# 7. Step 4 — Bespoke hazard thresholds using pSSD++ (ToMEx2.0_EcoToxRisk)

## 7.1 Toxicity dataset

Start with aligned toxicity records for freshwater species (i.e., quality-screened ToMEx 2.0 records aligned to both food dilution and tissue-translocation ERMs using bioaccessibility models and particle traits).

```{r load-tox-data}
# filter species by environment
tox_data <- tomex2 |> 
   dplyr::filter(
    env_f == "Freshwater",
    Group != "Bacterium", # Drop studies with Bacterium group
    Group != "Plant", # Drop studies with Plant group
    effect.metric != "HONEC", # Drop studies with HONEC effect metric
    tier_zero_tech_f == "Red Criteria Passed", #minimum QC for technical criteria
    tier_zero_risk_f == "Red Criteria Passed", #minimum QC for risk criteria
    risk.13 != 0 #Drop studies that received a score of 0 for endpoints criteria (this also drops studies that have not yet been)
  )

# summarize by group, species, and polymer type to understand tox data included in model
tox_data |> 
  group_by(Group, Species, poly_f, shape_f) |> 
  summarise(n = n(), .groups = "drop")
```

## 7.2 Hazard-side particle-trait parameter matrix

**SPEC 1b correction (differential vs. cumulative volume/area slope).** The particle-trait alignment parameters `a.v.*` (volume) and `a.sa.*` (surface area) in `PSSDplusplus::param_default_values` use the same **differential** ERM-slope convention as the length parameter `alpha.*` — consistent with the Kooi et al. (2021) mean-ERM formula and the Koelmans et al. (2020)/Coffin et al. (2022) rescaling equation (Section 5.1). A prior version of this analysis passed the **cumulative** C-PSD slope (`$a_cpsd`) into `a.v.*`/`a.sa.*` instead of the differential slope (`$a_psd = a_cpsd - 1`), leaving these parameters exactly 1.0 too shallow. Because the pSSD++ Food Dilution model computes a volumetric dose from the polydisperse mean particle volume, and the mean of a power-law distribution is acutely sensitive to how far the exponent is above or below 1, this ~1.0 shortfall in `a.v` inflated the mean particle volume — and therefore the Food Dilution risk quotient — by several orders of magnitude relative to the corrected value. `a.m.*` (mass) is set consistently with `a.v.*` below, since mass is proportional to volume at constant density; the two are asserted to agree within 0.3 as an internal consistency check. This correction is confined to the hazard-side alignment parameters; the exposure-side `correction_factor()` count rescaling (Section 5.1) already used the length-based differential slope only and is unaffected.

```{r}
# replace the default parameter matrix distribution with values derived using the C-PSD method here
param_values <- PSSDplusplus::param_default_values |>
  # update parameters from C-PSD method
  mutate(alpha.freshwater = -alpha_mu, # positive magnitude of differential a_psd where dN/dL = k * L^a
         alpha.freshwater.sd = alpha_se,
         # additional values need updating:
         ### Length to width ratio
         R.ave.water.freshwater = R.ave_mean,
         R.ave.water.freshwater.sd = R.ave_sd,

         ### polymer density
         #p.ave.freshwater = ,
         #p.ave.freshwater.sd = ,

         ### volume (SPEC 1b: differential a_psd = a_cpsd - 1, not the cumulative a_cpsd;
         ### the cumulative slope is exactly 1.0 too shallow and inflates the
         ### polydisperse mean particle volume, deflating the Food Dilution threshold)
         a.v.freshwater = -cpsd_fit_volume$a_psd,
         a.v.freshwater.sd = cpsd_fit_volume$se_a_psd,

         ### mass (mass ~ density * volume; at constant density this shares volume's
         ### differential slope, so set from data for consistency with a.v rather than
         ### retaining the unrelated package default, which would leave a.v/a.m mismatched)
         a.m.freshwater = -cpsd_fit_volume$a_psd,
         a.m.freshwater.sd = cpsd_fit_volume$se_a_psd,

         ### surface area
         a.sa.freshwater = -cpsd_fit_area$a_psd,# derived value for all shapes
         a.sa.freshwater.sd = cpsd_fit_area$se_a_psd
         )

# SPEC 1b acceptance check: a.v and a.m must be mutually consistent (mass ~ volume
# at constant density); flag rather than silently pass if they diverge materially.
stopifnot(abs(param_values$a.v.freshwater - param_values$a.m.freshwater) < 0.3)

# generate parameter matrix using bespoke environmental parameter values
set.seed(7001)
param_matrix <- matrix_function(
  n = n_boot, #size of matrix (10,000 is recommended)
  params = param_values, #parameter distribution values 
  #params = PSSDplusplus::param_default_values, #beta-test with defaults
  upper.tissue.truncation.limit = 500, # maximum particle size (microns) to truncate tissue tranlocation size limit distribution to based on biological plausibility
  x1M_set = 1, #minimum particle size to generate distributions to in microns
  x2D_set = 5000 #maximum particle size to generate distributions to in microns
) |> 
  # replace R.ave.water.freshwater with bootstrapped values
   mutate(R.ave.water.freshwater = sample(R.ave_vals, size = n(), replace = TRUE),
          H_W_ratio.freshwater = sample(R.ave_vals, size = n(), replace = TRUE)) #H_W ratio is assumed same as length-width ratio

# visualize parameter distributions
param_plots <- parameter_histograms_function(param_matrix) # generate parameter distribution plots
#visualize plots
alpha_combined_plot_river <- param_plots$alpha_combined_plot # distribution of alpha parameters
alpha_combined_plot_river <- label_matrix(alpha_combined_plot_river, "River water")

ggsave(alpha_combined_plot_river, filename = "figures/alpha_combined_plot_river.png", width = 9, height = 6, dpi = 300)
alpha_combined_plot_river
```

## 7.3 Run Monte-Carlo Simulation on Toxicity Data using Parameter Matrix

`MC_sim_align_parallel()` is the core PSSDplusplus function that aligns each toxicological endpoint to the **particle trait distributions** defined in `param_matrix`. For each Monte Carlo replicate ($i = 1, \ldots, n_\text{sim}$) it:

1. **Draws a particle trait vector** from `param_matrix`: particle size ($L$, log-normal), aspect ratio ($AR$), density ($\rho$), and C-PSD slope ($\alpha_\text{cpsd}$).
2. **Applies the bioaccessibility model** for each ERM:
   - *Food Dilution* — computes the volumetric food dilution dose (particles/L) using the particle volume and the organism's gut volume, converting the reported NOEC/EC dose to an environmentally comparable particle concentration.
   - *Tissue Translocation* — computes the particle flux to tissue using the size-dependent translocation model; only particles below the translocation size threshold (500 µm) are included.
3. **Aligns each species' EC dose** to a common concentration unit (particles/L equivalent), enabling a multi-species SSD to be constructed from studies that used different MP sizes, shapes, and concentrations.

The output `MC_sim_df` is a long data frame with one row per toxicological endpoint per Monte Carlo replicate, with columns for the aligned dose (`particles_L_food_dilution`, `particles_L_ox_stress`), bioaccessibility group (`ingestible`, `translocatable`), and quality tier (`risk.13`, `bio_f`). It is then split by ERM and filtered to the relevant endpoints before SSD fitting in Section 7.4.

```{r run-pssd-pipeline}
# run_pssd_pipeline() (sourced from R/mp_risk_utils.R) bundles MC_sim_align_parallel(),
# the ERM-specific results_df filtering, erm_registry construction, and make_all_pSSDs()
# into one step used identically across river/sediment/ocean.
river_pssd <- run_pssd_pipeline(
  tox_data     = tox_data,
  param_matrix = param_matrix,
  environments = c("Freshwater"),
  cache_suffix = "river",
  dose_unit    = "L",
  n_sim        = n_boot,
  num_cores    = parallel::detectCores() - 2,
  sim          = 30,
  cv_uf        = 0.5,
  rmore_method = "lognormal",
  seed         = 5001
)
MC_sim_df    <- river_pssd$MC_sim_df
erm_registry <- river_pssd$erm_registry
```

The output `MC_sim_df` is a long data frame with one row per toxicological endpoint per Monte Carlo replicate, with columns for the aligned dose (`particles_L_food_dilution`, `particles_L_ox_stress`), bioaccessibility group (`ingestible`, `translocatable`), and quality tier (`risk.13`, `bio_f`). It is split by ERM into `erm_registry` (Food Dilution / Tissue Translocation subsets) before SSD fitting below.

# 8. Step 5 — Risk characterization using joint distributions (Monte Carlo)

We now combine: - **Exposure**: bootstrap distribution (e.g., EED 50th percentile) or full empirical sample distribution. - **Hazard**: pSSD++-derived HC5/HC10 distributions for each ERM.

A common probabilistic risk metric is: - **Risk Quotient (RQ)**: `RQ = Exposure / Hazard`. - **Probability of exceedance**: `P(RQ > 1)`.

Below we compute four RQ distributions: [Food dilution, Tissue translocation] x [HC5, HC10].

```{r risk-quotient-1d}
# draw_rq_mc1d() and summarize_rq() are sourced from R/mp_risk_utils.R.
n_risk     <- 1000
set.seed(9301)
risk_draws <- draw_rq_mc1d(haz, eed_boot$q50, n_risk = n_risk)
risk_summary <- summarize_rq(risk_draws)
risk_summary
```

```{r rq-plot}
ggsave(rq_plot, filename = "figures/rq_plot.png", width = 9, height = 6, dpi = 300)
rq_plot
```

```{r risk-inline, include=FALSE}
rs_tissue_hc5  <- dplyr::filter(risk_summary, ERM == "Tissue Translocation", HCx == 5)
```

The 1D Monte Carlo risk characterization indicates a median RQ of `r round(rs_food_hc5$RQ_p50, 3)` for the Food Dilution ERM (HC5; P(RQ>1) = `r round(rs_food_hc5$P_exceed * 100, 1)`%) and `r round(rs_tissue_hc5$RQ_p50, 3)` for the Tissue Translocation ERM (HC5; P(RQ>1) = `r round(rs_tissue_hc5$P_exceed * 100, 1)`%). RQ values below 1 indicate exposure concentrations below the hazard threshold for the majority of aquatic species.

# 9. Two-dimensional Monte Carlo (MC2D)
**Two-dimensional Monte Carlo (MC2D)** to separately handle:
    -   *uncertainty* (e.g., correction factors, hazard model uncertainty),
    -   *variability* (true spatial/temporal variability in exposure).

Below, the **outer loop** samples uncertain parameters (a correction factor draw and one hazard draw per ERM/HCx),
while the **inner loop** samples exposure variability from the observed monitoring concentrations.

**How to read the MC2D outputs**

- Each *outer* iteration represents one plausible “world” of uncertainty (sampling one CF draw and one hazard draw per ERM/HCx).
- Within that world, the *inner* loop samples exposure variability across sites/dates (using the observed measured concentrations).
- For each outer iteration, we summarize the resulting RQ distribution as `P_exceed`, `RQ_p50`, `RQ_p95`, and `RQ_p99`.
- The distribution of these summaries across iterations quantifies **uncertainty in risk metrics**, while the inner loop represents **variability in exposure**.

```{r mc2d}
# mc2d_risk() is sourced from R/mp_risk_utils.R.
# Outer loop: n_uncertainty = 300 CF + hazard draws (uncertainty).
# Inner loop: n_variability = 1000 exposure draws per outer iteration (variability).
mc2d_results <- mc2d_risk(
  monitoring_df = monitoring,
  combined_cf   = combined_cf,
  haz_df        = haz,
  n_uncertainty = 300,
  n_variability = 1000,
  seed          = 1
)

mc2d_summary <- mc2d_results |>
  dplyr::group_by(ERM, HCx) |>
  summarise(
    P_exceed_med = median(P_exceed),
    P_exceed_p95 = quantile(P_exceed, 0.95),
    P_exceed_p05 = quantile(P_exceed, 0.05),
    RQ_p50_med = median(RQ_p50),
    RQ_p95_med = median(RQ_p95),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

mc2d_summary
```

```{r mc2d-pexceed-hist-plot}
ggsave(mc2d_pexceed_hist_plot, filename = "figures/mc2d_pexceed_hist_plot.png", width = 9, height = 6, dpi = 300)
mc2d_pexceed_hist_plot
```


# 10. Sensitivity analysis
**Sensitivity analysis** to identify dominant uncertainty contributors (e.g., alpha, plastic proportion, analytical recovery).

## 10.0 Hoffman et al. (2026) transport and slope-structure diagnostics

Hoffman et al. (2026) show that vertical transport can make a sampled PSD deviate from a single power law, with apparent slopes differing from the underlying PSD by about two exponent units across a critical size. The following diagnostics are model-based sensitivities. They do not replace the production CF, but they show how much the Food Dilution and Tissue Translocation risk summaries move when the slope uncertainty is widened beyond OLS fit error and when surface/subsurface samples are analyzed separately.

```{r hoffman-slope-uncertainty-sensitivity}
summarize_mc2d_hc5 <- function(x) {
  x |>
    dplyr::filter(HCx == 5) |>
    dplyr::group_by(ERM, HCx) |>
    dplyr::summarise(
      P_exceed_med = median(P_exceed),
      RQ_p50_med = median(RQ_p50),
      RQ_p95_med = median(RQ_p95),
      .groups = "drop"
    )
}

slope_sd_grid <- c(0, slope_structural_sd, 0.5, 1.0)
hoffman_slope_sensitivity <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(slope_sd_grid, function(sd_i) {
  set.seed(1000 + as.integer(sd_i * 1000))
  alpha_i <- alpha_dist(
    mu = cpsd_fit_all$a_psd,
    sd = cpsd_fit_all$se_a_psd,
    n = 3000,
    structural_sd = sd_i
  )
  cf_i <- correction_factor(
    a = alpha_i,
    L_meas_min = L_meas_min_use,
    L_meas_max = L_meas_max_use,
    L_tar_min = 1,
    L_tar_max = 5000,
    slope_convention = "differential"
  )
  mc_i <- mc2d_risk(
    monitoring_df = monitoring,
    combined_cf = cf_i,
    haz_df = haz,
    n_uncertainty = 100,
    n_variability = 500,
    seed = 2000 + as.integer(sd_i * 1000)
  )
  summarize_mc2d_hc5(mc_i) |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      structural_sd = sd_i,
      CF_p50 = median(cf_i),
      CF_p95 = quantile(cf_i, 0.95)
    )
}))

knitr::kable(
  hoffman_slope_sensitivity,
  digits = 3,
  caption = "SPEC 2 sensitivity: river HC5 risk response to widened differential-slope structural uncertainty"
)
```

The `structural_sd = 0` row isolates the corrected differential-slope convention with fit uncertainty only. Wider rows are assumptions motivated by Hoffman et al. (2026) and the RIVM (2025) precedent for deliberately broad slope priors; they are sampled in the MC2D outer uncertainty loop through `combined_cf`, not in the inner exposure-variability loop.

```{r hoffman-depth-stratified-sensitivity}
depth_levels <- levels(monitoring$sample_depth_general)

depth_shape_fits <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(depth_levels, function(depth_i) {
  dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(c("fragment", "fiber", "all"), function(shape_i) {
    dat_i <- raw_particles_river |> dplyr::filter(sample_depth_general == depth_i)
    if (shape_i != "all") dat_i <- dat_i |> dplyr::filter(shape == shape_i)
    vals <- dat_i |> dplyr::pull(length_um)
    fit_i <- fit_cpsd_segur_r(vals, bin_um = 5)
    tibble::tibble(
      sample_depth_general = depth_i,
      shape = shape_i,
      n_particles = length(vals),
      a_cpsd = fit_i$a_cpsd,
      a_psd = fit_i$a_psd,
      se_a_psd = fit_i$se_a_psd,
      lod_low_um = fit_i$lower_lod_used_um,
      lod_high_um = fit_i$upper_lod_um,
      r2 = fit_i$r2
    )
  }))
}))

depth_slope_plot <- depth_shape_fits |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(x = sample_depth_general, y = a_psd, color = shape)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 3, position = ggplot2::position_dodge(width = 0.35)) +
  ggplot2::geom_errorbar(
    ggplot2::aes(ymin = a_psd - se_a_psd, ymax = a_psd + se_a_psd),
    width = 0.15,
    position = ggplot2::position_dodge(width = 0.35)
  ) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "Sampling depth stratum",
    y = expression(italic(a)[psd]),
    title = "River C-PSD slope by sampling depth and shape"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 18)

ggsave(depth_slope_plot, filename = "figures/hoffman_depth_slope_plot.png", width = 9, height = 6, dpi = 300)
depth_slope_plot

depth_sensitivity <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(depth_levels, function(depth_i) {
  fit_row <- depth_shape_fits |>
    dplyr::filter(sample_depth_general == depth_i, shape == "all") |>
    dplyr::slice(1)
  fit_i <- fit_cpsd_segur_r(
    raw_particles_river |>
      dplyr::filter(sample_depth_general == depth_i) |>
      dplyr::pull(length_um),
    bin_um = 5
  )
  alpha_i <- alpha_dist(
    mu = fit_i$a_psd,
    sd = fit_i$se_a_psd,
    n = 3000,
    structural_sd = slope_structural_sd
  )
  mon_i <- monitoring |> dplyr::filter(sample_depth_general == depth_i)
  corr_i <- correct_and_bootstrap_eed(
    monitoring = mon_i,
    conc_col = "C_measured_pL",
    cpsd_fit = fit_i,
    alpha_draws = alpha_i,
    L_tar_min = 1,
    L_tar_max = 5000,
    n_draws = 1000,
    n_boot = n_boot,
    probs = c(0.5, 0.95),
    slope_convention = "differential"
  )
  mc_i <- mc2d_risk(
    monitoring_df = corr_i$monitoring,
    combined_cf = corr_i$combined_cf,
    haz_df = haz,
    n_uncertainty = 100,
    n_variability = 500,
    seed = 3000 + match(depth_i, depth_levels)
  )
  summarize_mc2d_hc5(mc_i) |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      sample_depth_general = depth_i,
      n_monitoring = nrow(mon_i),
      a_psd = fit_i$a_psd,
      CF_p50 = median(corr_i$combined_cf),
      EED_q50_p50 = median(corr_i$eed_boot$q50),
      EED_q95_p50 = median(corr_i$eed_boot$q95)
    )
}))

knitr::kable(
  depth_sensitivity,
  digits = 3,
  caption = "SPEC 3 river depth-stratified sensitivity for corrected EED and HC5 risk"
)
```

Surface and subsurface strata are both large enough to fit C-PSD slopes and bootstrap monitoring observations. The headline assessment remains pooled because this is a screening ERA and the transport correction is not yet mechanistic; the stratified rows are retained as a sensitivity that can identify whether boundary-enriched samples materially alter EED or RQ.

## 10.1 Morris global sensitivity analysis (future work)

A Morris elementary-effects screen (global sensitivity ranking of RQ uncertainty drivers) is deferred to a dedicated compute pass: it repeatedly rebuilds small pSSD++ hazard models and, at a budget large enough to produce a stable ranking, is too slow for a routine report render. It did not run in this render.


## 10.2 µFTIR objective: critical assessment of the detection floor and its intersection with the LOD/CF workflow

### Instrument configuration

The µFTIR analysis used an objective equivalent to ~4× magnification with **25 µm pixel size**. At this pixel resolution, the practical minimum detectable particle size (requiring ≥ 2 pixels across the shortest dimension) is approximately **50 µm** — consistent with the `L_meas_min = 50 µm` parameter used throughout this workflow. This value is **already embedded in the correction factor (CF) calculation** and is not an additional bias to correct.

### Why the Wang et al. (2026) ×33 scaling factor does not apply here

Wang et al. (2026) found that a 4× µFTIR objective (20 µm pixel) detects only 3 ± 3% of particles relative to a 25× reference (2 µm pixel). At face value this suggests a ×33 upward scaling should be applied to our concentrations. **This is incorrect for the following reasons:**

**1. The 97% "missed" particles lie almost entirely below our measurement floor.**

The 25× objective in Wang et al. detects particles as small as ~4 µm. The 4× objective detects only those ≥ ~40–50 µm. The difference (97% of total particle count) is dominated by particles in the 4–50 µm size class. Our workflow already treats `L_meas_min = 50 µm` as the lower detection floor and uses the power-law CF to extrapolate particle counts from this floor down to 1 µm. The Wang et al. sub-50 µm particles are not "missing" from our analysis — they are the precise population that the `correction_factor()` function reconstructs via power-law integration.

**2. Within the measured range (50–500 µm), the 4×/25 µm system is effective.**

At 25 µm pixel size:

| Particle size | Pixels across | Detection status |
|---|---|---|
| 50 µm | 2 px | Marginal (meets minimum) |
| 100 µm | 4 px | Reliable |
| 200 µm | 8 px | Well-resolved |
| 500 µm | 20 px | Fully resolved |

For particles at or above 100 µm — which covers the entire Segur LOD fitting window (fragments: `r round(cpsd_fit_frag$lower_lod_used_um)`–`r round(cpsd_fit_frag$upper_lod_um)` µm; all shapes: `r round(cpsd_fit_all$lower_lod_used_um)`–`r round(cpsd_fit_all$upper_lod_um)` µm) — detection is reliable with this pixel size. The ×33 correction factor was derived from total particle counts including the sub-50 µm population; it does not represent within-range inefficiency.

**3. The Segur LOD algorithm implicitly handles the marginal 50–100 µm zone.**

The Segur LOD search specifically identifies the size window where the C-PSD is most linear ($R^2 \geq 0.90$). The 50–100 µm region, where detection by the 4×/25 µm system may be incomplete, would manifest as a deviation from power-law behavior at the lower end of the binned distribution — and would therefore be *excluded* from the fitting window. Indeed, the fitted lower LODs (`r round(cpsd_fit_frag$lower_lod_used_um)` µm for fragments, `r round(cpsd_fit_all$lower_lod_used_um)` µm pooled) are well above 50 µm, confirming that the algorithm already pushed the lower bound into the reliable detection zone.

**4. Applying ×33 on top of the existing CF would double-count.**

The current CF has a median of `r round(median(combined_cf), 1)`× (90% CI: `r round(quantile(combined_cf, 0.05), 1)`–`r round(quantile(combined_cf, 0.95), 1)`×). This already accounts for the unmeasured sub-50 µm population via power-law extrapolation. Multiplying `C_corrected` by an additional 33× would apply a second, conflicting correction to the same particle pool, producing a total inflation factor of ~`r round(median(combined_cf) * 33, 0)`× — far in excess of any defensible estimate.

### Residual uncertainty: the 50–100 µm marginal zone

The one genuine uncertainty from the 4×/25 µm configuration is **incomplete counting in the 50–100 µm particle size class**. Particles in this range occupy 2–4 pixels and may be undercounted by approximately 10–30% relative to what a 15× system would detect. The sensitivity analysis below quantifies the effect of adjusting `L_meas_min` from 50 µm to 100 µm, which effectively removes the marginal zone from the measured concentration estimate and lets the CF extrapolate it instead.

```{r lmeas-sensitivity, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Compare CF and risk outcomes under two L_meas_min assumptions:
# 50 µm (current, includes marginal zone) vs 100 µm (excludes marginal zone — conservative floor)
lmeas_scenarios <- list(
  "L_meas_min = 50 µm (current)" = list(L_lo = 50,  L_hi = 500),
  "L_meas_min = 100 µm (conservative)" = list(L_lo = 100, L_hi = 500)
)

lmeas_cf_summary <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(lmeas_scenarios), function(scen) {
  s   <- lmeas_scenarios[[scen]]
  cf_s <- correction_factor(
    a           = alpha,                  # differential a_psd draws (n_mc)
    L_meas_min  = s$L_lo,
    L_meas_max  = s$L_hi,
    L_tar_min   = 1,
    L_tar_max   = 5000,
    slope_convention = "differential"
  )
  data.frame(
    scenario = scen,
    CF_p05   = round(quantile(cf_s, 0.05),  1),
    CF_med   = round(median(cf_s),           1),
    CF_p95   = round(quantile(cf_s, 0.95),  1)
  )
}))

knitr::kable(lmeas_cf_summary,
  caption = paste0(
    "Correction factor (50–500 µm → 1–5000 µm) under alternative lower detection limits. ",
    "Using differential a_psd = ", round(cpsd_fit_all$a_psd, 3), " (all shapes, Segur LOD). ",
    "n_mc = ", n_mc, " Monte Carlo draws."
  ),
  col.names = c("Scenario", "CF 5th pct", "CF median", "CF 95th pct")
)
```

```{r lmeas-inline, include=FALSE}
cf_50  <- lmeas_cf_summary$CF_med[lmeas_cf_summary$scenario == "L_meas_min = 50 µm (current)"]
cf_100 <- lmeas_cf_summary$CF_med[lmeas_cf_summary$scenario == "L_meas_min = 100 µm (conservative)"]
```

Raising `L_meas_min` from 50 to 100 µm increases the median CF from `r cf_50`× to `r cf_100`× — a modest change that reflects the additional particles in the 50–100 µm range being moved from "measured" to "extrapolated." This is the appropriate sensitivity analysis for this instrument configuration: it brackets the range of outcomes depending on whether the marginal detection zone is treated as reliably measured or excluded and reconstructed via power-law. The current workflow (`L_meas_min = 50 µm`) is the less conservative (lower CF) choice; if the 50–100 µm counts are systematically low due to detection limits, the true concentration may be closer to the `L_meas_min = 100 µm` estimate.

**Summary.** No additional objective-based correction factor is applied to `C_measured_pL`. The existing workflow already accounts for instrument detection limits through (1) the `L_meas_min = 50 µm` floor that reflects the 4×/25 µm pixel detection limit, and (2) the power-law CF that extrapolates particle counts from this floor to the 1 µm target. The Segur LOD fitting window (≥ `r round(cpsd_fit_all$lower_lod_used_um)` µm) lies entirely within the reliable detection zone of the instrument. The Wang et al. (2026) ×33 factor would be appropriate only if converting a 4× total particle count to an equivalent 25× total count *without* any power-law extrapolation — not in combination with the CF approach used here.

# 11. Sediment — Beach Sand

## 11.1 Derive power-law values from raw sediment particle data

```{r}
# import sediment particle data (beach sand as sediment proxy)
raw_particles_sed <- raw_particles |> 
  dplyr::filter(sample_type == "beach sand") |>
  assign_polymer_density(lookup = polymer_density_tbl)

# ---- Thickness (height) factor from sediment data ----
ratio_tbl_sed <- raw_particles_sed |>
  mutate(
    WL = 1 / aspect_ratio,
    width_eff_um = case_when(
      shape == "fragment" & !is.na(area_um2) & !is.na(length_um) & length_um > 0 &
        !is.na(circularity) & circularity < 0.7 ~ area_um2 / length_um,
      TRUE ~ width_um
    )
  ) |> 
  group_by(shape) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    r_med  = median(WL, na.rm = TRUE),
    r_low  = quantile(WL, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    r_high = quantile(WL, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# ---- Volumes ----
raw_particles_sed <- raw_particles_sed |>
  left_join(ratio_tbl_sed |> dplyr::select(shape, r_med), by = "shape") |>  
  mutate(
    height_um = r_med * width_um,
    V_um3 = case_when(
      shape == "fragment" ~ (pi / 6) * length_um * width_um * height_um,
      shape == "fiber"    ~ pi * (width_um / 2)^2 * length_um,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_
    ),
    mass_ug = V_um3 * density_g_cm3,
    mass_ug_fixed_density_1.1 = V_um3 * 1.1
  )
```

### Particle length
```{r cpsd-fits-sed-length}
cpsd_fits_sed_length <- fit_cpsd_by_shape(
  raw_particles_sed, value_col = "length_um",
  config = list(
    fragment = list(bin_um = 5, fit_range_um = c(NA_real_, NA_real_)),
    fiber    = list(bin_um = 5, fit_range_um = c(NA_real_, NA_real_)),
    all      = list(bin_um = 5, fit_range_um = c(NA_real_, NA_real_))
  )
)
cpsd_fit_sed_frag  <- cpsd_fits_sed_length$fragment
cpsd_fit_sed_fiber <- cpsd_fits_sed_length$fiber
cpsd_fit_sed_all   <- cpsd_fits_sed_length$all

set.seed(8002)
alpha_sed <- alpha_dist(
  mu = cpsd_fit_sed_all$a_psd,
  sd = cpsd_fit_sed_all$se_a_psd,
  n = 20000,
  structural_sd = slope_structural_sd
)

alpha_sed_mu <- mean(alpha_sed)
alpha_sed_se <- sd(alpha_sed)

cat("Sediment All: alpha =", signif(cpsd_fit_sed_all$a_cpsd, 2), "+-", signif(cpsd_fit_sed_all$se_a_cpsd, 2),
    ", LOD =", signif(cpsd_fit_sed_all$lower_lod_used_um, 2), "–", signif(cpsd_fit_sed_all$upper_lod_um, 2), "µm\n")
```

### Particle volume

`volume_particle()`-derived LOD bounds (same shape-dependent geometry as river, Section
4.2.3), so the sediment volume C-PSD fit uses the same rigor as river's fragment/fiber
fits rather than one flat `bin_um` with no LOD-bounds constraint.

```{r sed-volume-lod-bounds}
# volume_lod_bounds() (sourced from R/mp_risk_utils.R) — see the river volume-lod-bounds
# chunk (Section 4.2.3) for the rationale: length/width-consistent bounds via the measured
# r_med ratio, rather than an isotropic (L=W=H) assumption.
r_med_frag_sed  <- ratio_tbl_sed$r_med[ratio_tbl_sed$shape == "fragment"]
r_med_fiber_sed <- ratio_tbl_sed$r_med[ratio_tbl_sed$shape == "fiber"]
vlb_sed <- volume_lod_bounds(cpsd_fit_sed_frag, cpsd_fit_sed_fiber, r_med_frag_sed, r_med_fiber_sed)
cat("Sediment fragment volume LOD: [", signif(vlb_sed$fragment[1], 2), ",", signif(vlb_sed$fragment[2], 2), "] µm³\n")
cat("Sediment fiber    volume LOD: [", signif(vlb_sed$fiber[1],    2), ",", signif(vlb_sed$fiber[2],    2), "] µm³\n")
cat("Sediment all      volume LOD: [", signif(vlb_sed$all[1],      2), ",", signif(vlb_sed$all[2],      2), "] µm³\n")
```
