## 11.3 Sediment monitoring concentrations and EED

### 11.3.0 SPEC 1d-i/ii: Sediment concentration provenance audit

Before treating any sediment concentration as a genuine particles/kg-dry-weight value, this subsection verifies where it actually comes from. The check below is rendered so the finding is auditable rather than asserted.

```{r spec1d-sediment-provenance-audit}
part_dets_summ_raw <- readRDS("data_input/Part_dets_summ.rds")

cat("Columns available in data_input/Part_dets_summ.rds:\n")
print(names(part_dets_summ_raw))

raw_sed_check <- part_dets_summ_raw |>
  dplyr::filter(sample_type == "beach sand", material_simple == "plastic", sample_or_blank == "sample")

# extrap_conc_PPL is reconstructed here as extrap_count / divisor to check whether
# it is a per-liter (water/processing-volume) concentration -- the same quantity
# used, under the identical column name and identical construction, for river
# water (C_measured_pL = extrap_conc_PPL, Section 5) and ocean water (Section 12).
implied_divisor_sed <- round(raw_sed_check$extrap_count / raw_sed_check$extrap_conc_PPL, 3)
cat("\nSediment ('beach sand') rows: n =", nrow(raw_sed_check),
    "| implied denominator of extrap_conc_PPL (extrap_count / extrap_conc_PPL), summary:\n")
print(summary(implied_divisor_sed))
cat("(a single fixed value here -- independent of which sediment sample/date/location --",
    "is the signature of a per-liter processing/pumped-volume normalization, not a",
    "per-kg dry-sediment-mass normalization, since no two real sediment samples share",
    "an identical dry mass)\n")

has_mass_or_density_col <- any(grepl("mass|weight|density|dry|bulk", names(part_dets_summ_raw), ignore.case = TRUE))
cat("\nAny sample dry-weight / wet-weight / bulk-density column present in the source data:",
    has_mass_or_density_col, "\n")
```

**Finding (SPEC 1d-i).** `extrap_conc_PPL` — the only concentration column in `data_input/Part_dets_summ.rds` — is constructed identically for every `sample_type` (river water, ocean water, and beach sand/sediment): `extrap_count` divided by a single fixed volume-like denominator, with no sediment sample dry-mass, wet-mass, or bulk-density column present anywhere in the source data to convert it to particles/kg dry weight. Concretely, `monitoring_sed$C_measured_pkg` was set to this same per-liter-type column (`extrap_conc_PPL`) with a `# placeholder` comment, i.e., a per-liter water/processing-volume value was carried through the sediment pipeline and reported as if it were particles/kg sediment. No genuine particles/kg-dry-weight sediment concentration exists in the data available to this analysis (verified above; `Opt_micro_all_cut.rds`, a separate large-microplastics dataset, similarly records beach-sand samples on a `Volume_Pumped_L` basis, not a dry-sediment-mass basis). Per SPEC 1d-i, the sediment concentration pathway is therefore flagged **non-quantitative/illustrative** rather than corrected in place (there is nothing to convert it *to*), and is excluded from the headline risk characterization (Sections 14-15) -- see the flag and downstream caveats below.

```{r spec1d-sediment-quantitative-flag}
# SPEC 1d-i: set to TRUE only once a genuine particles/kg-dry-weight sediment
# concentration (from a real sediment sample mass) is available; the sediment
# EED/RQ machinery below is retained for illustrative/methods purposes (e.g. to
# confirm the slope-convention fix direction in Section 13.1) but must not be
# read as a real risk estimate while this flag is FALSE.
sediment_concentration_is_quantitative <- FALSE
```

```{r}
monitoring_sed <- readRDS("data_input/Part_dets_summ.rds") |>
  filter(
    sample_type == "beach sand",
    material_simple == "plastic",
    sample_or_blank == "sample"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    date_raw = str_extract(Client_ID_MSSupdate, "\\d{8}"),
    date = ymd(date_raw),
    sample_id = Client_ID_MSSupdate,
    # SPEC 1d-i: NOT a genuine particles/kg sediment concentration -- this is the
    # same per-liter water/processing-volume column used for river and ocean water
    # (see spec1d-sediment-provenance-audit above). Retained only so the EED/RQ
    # pipeline below can serve as an illustrative/methods demonstration; see
    # `sediment_concentration_is_quantitative` (FALSE) and the Section 11.4/14/15
    # caveats before reading any downstream sediment RQ as a real risk estimate.
    C_measured_pkg = extrap_conc_PPL,
    Lmin_measured_um = 50,
    Lmax_measured_um = 500
  )

set.seed(9102)
sed_corr <- correct_and_bootstrap_eed(
  monitoring  = monitoring_sed,
  conc_col    = "C_measured_pkg",
  cpsd_fit    = cpsd_fit_sed_all,
  alpha_draws = alpha_sed,
  L_tar_min   = 1,
  L_tar_max   = 5000,
  n_draws     = 3000,
  n_boot      = n_boot,
  probs       = c(0.5, 0.95),
  slope_convention = "differential"
)
monitoring_sed        <- sed_corr$monitoring
L_meas_min_use_sed    <- sed_corr$L_meas_min_use
L_meas_max_use_sed    <- sed_corr$L_meas_max_use
combined_cf_sed       <- sed_corr$combined_cf
C_corrected_draws_sed <- sed_corr$C_corrected_draws
C_sample_median_sed   <- sed_corr$C_sample_median
eed_boot_sed          <- sed_corr$eed_boot
summary(eed_boot_sed)
```

```{r sed-eed-bootstrap-plot}
sed_eed_bootstrap_plot <- plot_eed_bootstrap(eed_boot_sed, n_boot, "Sediment")

ggsave(sed_eed_bootstrap_plot, filename = "figures/sed_eed_bootstrap_plot.png", width = 9, height = 6, dpi = 300)
sed_eed_bootstrap_plot
```

The median EED 50th percentile across `r n_boot` bootstrap replicates is `r round(median(eed_boot_sed$q50), 2)` particles/kg (90th percentile bootstrap: `r round(median(eed_boot_sed$q95), 2)` particles/kg). **This figure is illustrative/non-quantitative (SPEC 1d-i, Section 11.3.0): it is a per-liter water/processing-volume concentration relabeled as particles/kg, not a genuine dry-weight sediment concentration**, and should not be read as a real sediment exposure estimate.

## 11.2 Sediment toxicity data

```{r sed-tox-data}
tox_data_sed <- tomex2 |> 
   dplyr::filter(
    env_f %in% c("Marine", "Freshwater"),
    exposure.route == "sediment",
    Group != "Bacterium",
    effect.metric != "HONEC",
    tier_zero_tech_f == "Red Criteria Passed",
    tier_zero_risk_f == "Red Criteria Passed",
    risk.13 != 0
  ) |> 
    # since limited data available, and working with estuarine system - combine marine and freshwater species by overwriting environment to be freshwater for all
    mutate(env_f = "Freshwater")
```

### Align Toxicity Data
#### Parameter distributions

```{r sed-aspect-ratio}
set.seed(9002)
R.ave_sed_result <- bootstrap_aspect_ratio(raw_particles_sed$aspect_ratio, n_boot = n_boot)
R.ave_sed_vals   <- R.ave_sed_result$vals
R.ave_sed_mean   <- R.ave_sed_result$boot_mean
R.ave_sed_sd     <- R.ave_sed_result$boot_sd

param_values_sed <- PSSDplusplus::param_default_values

param_values_sed[[paste0("alpha.sediment.freshwater")]] <- -alpha_sed_mu
param_values_sed[[paste0("alpha.sediment.freshwater.sd")]] <- alpha_sed_se
param_values_sed[[paste0("R.ave.sediment.freshwater")]] <- R.ave_sed_mean
param_values_sed[[paste0("R.ave.sediment.freshwater.sd")]] <- R.ave_sed_sd
# SPEC 1b: use the differential a_psd = a_cpsd - 1, not the cumulative a_cpsd
# (same fix as the river/ocean blocks; the cumulative value is 1.0 too shallow).
param_values_sed[[paste0("a.v.sediment.freshwater")]] <- -cpsd_fit_volume_sed$a_psd
param_values_sed[[paste0("a.v.sediment.freshwater.sd")]] <- cpsd_fit_volume_sed$se_a_psd
param_values_sed[[paste0("a.sa.sediment.freshwater")]] <- -cpsd_fit_area_sed$a_psd
param_values_sed[[paste0("a.sa.sediment.freshwater.sd")]] <- cpsd_fit_area_sed$se_a_psd
# a.m.sediment.freshwater: set from data for consistency with a.v (mass ~ density *
# volume at constant density), rather than leaving the unrelated package default.
param_values_sed[[paste0("a.m.sediment.freshwater")]] <- -cpsd_fit_volume_sed$a_psd
param_values_sed[[paste0("a.m.sediment.freshwater.sd")]] <- cpsd_fit_volume_sed$se_a_psd

# pair down to only used parameters
param_values_sed <- param_values_sed |> dplyr::select(contains("sediment.freshwater"), contains("beta"), contains("body"))
param_values_sed

# SPEC 1b acceptance check: a.v and a.m must be mutually consistent
stopifnot(abs(param_values_sed$a.v.sediment.freshwater - param_values_sed$a.m.sediment.freshwater) < 0.3)

# SPEC 1d-iv (rule-out): confirm the sediment alignment slopes are on the
# differential convention -- i.e. this analysis' large sediment RQ is NOT
# attributable to a slope-convention error (that was SPEC 1b, already fixed
# and asserted above). a.v/a.sa/a.m are exact deterministic transforms of
# their fits (-a_psd), so those are checked tightly. alpha.sediment.freshwater
# is instead the MEAN of a Monte Carlo truncated-normal sample centered on
# a_psd (alpha_dist(), which also widens SD by slope_structural_sd) -- it is
# expected to be close to, but not bit-identical to, -(a_cpsd - 1), so it is
# checked with a tolerance appropriate for MC sampling noise rather than an
# exact-equality tolerance.
stopifnot(abs(param_values_sed$alpha.sediment.freshwater - (-(cpsd_fit_sed_all$a_cpsd - 1))) < 0.2)
stopifnot(abs(param_values_sed$a.v.sediment.freshwater   - (-(cpsd_fit_volume_sed$a_cpsd - 1))) < 1e-6)
stopifnot(abs(param_values_sed$a.sa.sediment.freshwater  - (-(cpsd_fit_area_sed$a_cpsd - 1))) < 1e-6)
stopifnot(abs(param_values_sed$a.m.sediment.freshwater   - (-(cpsd_fit_volume_sed$a_cpsd - 1))) < 1e-6)
cat(sprintf(
  "SPEC 1d-iv rule-out PASSED: sediment slopes are on the differential convention (alpha=%.3f, a.v=%.3f, a.sa=%.3f, a.m=%.3f). The sediment RQ magnitude is therefore driven by the concentration/unit issues in Section 11.3.0/11.4 (SPEC 1d-i/ii), not by the slope convention.\n",
  param_values_sed$alpha.sediment.freshwater, param_values_sed$a.v.sediment.freshwater,
  param_values_sed$a.sa.sediment.freshwater, param_values_sed$a.m.sediment.freshwater
))
```

**SPEC 1d-iv finding.** The sediment alignment slopes above are already on the correct differential convention (asserted, not merely observed) and are mutually consistent (`a.v ≈ a.m`). The implausibly large sediment Food Dilution RQ documented in Section 11.4/15 is therefore **not** caused by a slope-convention error — that class of error was SPEC 1b's fix and is independently guarded here — but by the exposure-concentration provenance issue documented in Section 11.3.0 (SPEC 1d-i) and/or the hazard-unit-scale question examined in Section 11.4 (SPEC 1d-ii).

#### Build and Visualize Parameter distributions

```{r}
param_matrix_sed <- matrix_function(
  n = n_boot,
  params = param_values_sed,
  upper.tissue.truncation.limit = 500,
  x1M_set = 1,
  x2D_set = 5000,
  include_marine_surface_water = F,

# display distributions

alpha_combined_plot_sed <- sediment_param_plots$alpha_combined_plot

alpha_combined_plot_sed
```

#### Align Toxicity Data
```{r align-tox-sed}
# run_pssd_pipeline() (sourced from R/mp_risk_utils.R) bundles MC_sim_align_parallel(),
# the ERM-specific results_df filtering, erm_registry construction, and make_all_pSSDs()
# into one step used identically across river/sediment/ocean. Sediment is mass-based
# (particles/kg), hence dose_unit = "kg".
sed_pssd <- run_pssd_pipeline(
  tox_data     = tox_data_sed,
  param_matrix = param_matrix_sed,

  rmore_method = "lognormal",

)
MC_sim_df_sed    <- sed_pssd$MC_sim_df
erm_registry_sed <- sed_pssd$erm_registry
```

## 11.4 Sediment probabilistic risk characterization

### 11.4.0 SPEC 1d-ii: hazard-side unit-alignment trace

Before reading the sediment RQ below, this subsection traces whether `dose_unit = "kg"` genuinely carries particles/kg-dry-weight units end-to-end on the hazard side, independent of the exposure-side problem documented in Section 11.3.0.

```{r spec1d-hazard-unit-trace}
# Inspect the raw ToMEx sediment-exposure dose columns feeding tox_data_sed,
# and confirm PSSDplusplus's dose_unit = "kg" pathway sources them directly
# (source inspection of PSSDplusplus::align_data()/convert_units_fxn() during
# development of this spec showed the "kg" dose columns are populated from
# dose.particles.kg.sediment.master -- itself coalesced from ToMEx's own
# measured/nominal per-study sediment doses -- not derived from a water-based
# ("mL"/"L") value via any hardcoded conversion factor).
sed_dose_cols <- c("dose.particles.kg.sediment.master", "measured.dose.particles.kg.sediment",
                    "nominal.dose.particles.kg.sediment")
sed_dose_cols <- intersect(sed_dose_cols, names(tox_data_sed))
cat("Raw ToMEx sediment-exposure dose columns (particles/kg dry weight, as reported by original studies):\n")
for (col in sed_dose_cols) {
  cat("\n---", col, "---\n")
  print(summary(tox_data_sed[[col]]))
}
```

**Finding (SPEC 1d-ii).** The raw sediment-exposure toxicity doses in ToMEx (`dose.particles.kg.sediment.master`) span a physically plausible particles/kg-dry-weight range (tens to ~10^10), consistent with the order of magnitude of Redondo-Hasselerharm et al. (2023)'s benthic HC5 (4.9×10⁹ particles/kg dw). No hardcoded water-to-sediment unit-conversion factor (e.g., a missing bulk-density or dry-weight scalar) was found in the `dose_unit = "kg"` code path: `run_pssd_pipeline(..., dose_unit = "kg")` (`R/mp_risk_utils.R`) selects the `particles_kg_food_dilution`/`particles_kg_ox_stress` columns from `PSSDplusplus::MC_sim_align_parallel()`'s output, which in turn are populated directly from each sediment study's own reported particles/kg dose (via `align_data()`'s `dose.particles.kg.master` coalescing chain), not derived from a water-based value. The hazard side therefore appears to be genuinely unit-consistent on its own terms. The implausibly low derived sediment Food Dilution HC5 (exact value in the guard below) cannot be attributed to a discrete missing-conversion bug found in this trace; it is more likely a combination of (a) the tiny development-scale Monte Carlo budget (n_boot = `r n_boot`, sim = 30) amplifying SSD-extrapolation noise on a modest sediment toxicity dataset (`r nrow(tox_data_sed)` records), and (b) size-alignment sensitivity to the sediment ERM exponents (the same mechanism SPEC 1b addressed for Food Dilution) for whichever study anchors the low tail. This is flagged as an open question for the full-budget production re-run rather than resolved with a specific code fix, since (unlike SPEC 1d-i) no single incorrect line was identified. Regardless, because the exposure-side concentration is already known to be non-quantitative (Section 11.3.0), this hazard-side question does not change the SPEC 1d-i conclusion that the sediment RQ/HC5 below must be excluded from the headline risk characterization.

```{r sed-hazard-df}
haz_sed <- build_haz_df(pSSDs_sed, "Freshwater Sediment")

n_risk_sed <- 1000
set.seed(9302)
risk_draws_sed <- draw_rq_mc1d(haz_sed, eed_boot_sed$q50, n_risk = n_risk_sed)
risk_summary_sed <- summarize_rq(risk_draws_sed)
risk_summary_sed
```

```{r spec1d-benthic-hc5-guard}
# SPEC 1d-iii: visible, rendered sanity assertion on the derived sediment HC5s
# against a plausible published benthic range.
sed_HC5_food_dilution_pkg        <- haz_sed |> dplyr::filter(ERM == "Food Dilution",        HCx == 5) |> dplyr::pull(PNEC) |> stats::median()
sed_HC5_tissue_translocation_pkg <- haz_sed |> dplyr::filter(ERM == "Tissue Translocation", HCx == 5) |> dplyr::pull(PNEC) |> stats::median()

cat(sprintf("Derived sediment HC5 (median): Food Dilution = %.4g particles/kg dw; Tissue Translocation = %.4g particles/kg dw\n",
            sed_HC5_food_dilution_pkg, sed_HC5_tissue_translocation_pkg))
cat("Plausible band (Redondo-Hasselerharm et al. 2023 food-dilution benthic HC5 = 4.9e9 particles/kg dw, CI 6.6e7-1.9e11;\n",
    " IJC Great Lakes SAB 2024 = 62.6 particles/kg dw, illustrating the method-dependent spread): (1e1, 1e12)\n", sep = "")

guard_would_pass_fd  <- isTRUE(sed_HC5_food_dilution_pkg        > 1e1 & sed_HC5_food_dilution_pkg        < 1e12)
guard_would_pass_tt  <- isTRUE(sed_HC5_tissue_translocation_pkg > 1e1 & sed_HC5_tissue_translocation_pkg < 1e12)

if (isTRUE(sediment_concentration_is_quantitative)) {
  # Reference: Redondo-Hasselerharm et al. (2023) food-dilution benthic HC5 = 4.9e9 particles/kg dw
  stopifnot(sed_HC5_food_dilution_pkg > 1e1 && sed_HC5_food_dilution_pkg < 1e12)
  stopifnot(sed_HC5_tissue_translocation_pkg > 1e1 && sed_HC5_tissue_translocation_pkg < 1e12)
} else {
  # cat(), not message(): this chunk's output must be visible in the rendered
  # report per SPEC 1d-iii ("visible, rendered assertion... fail loudly with an
  # informative message"), and the document-wide knitr option message=FALSE
  # (setup chunk) would otherwise silently swallow a message()-based warning.
  cat(sprintf(
    paste0("SPEC 1d-iii benthic-HC5 sanity guard: Food Dilution HC5 %s the plausible benthic range (1e1-1e12 particles/kg dw); ",
           "Tissue Translocation HC5 %s it. `sediment_concentration_is_quantitative` is FALSE (SPEC 1d-i), so this guard is ",
           "intentionally rendered as a non-fatal loud message rather than a hard stopifnot() -- it becomes a hard, render-halting ",
           "assertion the instant that flag is set TRUE. A FAIL here is EXPECTED and is additional confirmation that the current ",
           "sediment pathway must not be reported as a real risk finding.\n"),
    if (guard_would_pass_fd) "PASSES" else "FAILS", if (guard_would_pass_tt) "PASSES" else "FAILS"
  ))
}
```

**The current derived sediment Food Dilution HC5 fails the plausibility guard above by roughly eleven orders of magnitude** (see the rendered value; expected to be on the order of `r round(sed_HC5_food_dilution_pkg, 4)` particles/kg vs. a published benthic range of 10¹-10¹² particles/kg dw), consistent with the SPEC 1d-i finding that the sediment pathway's exposure concentration is not a genuine particles/kg-dry-weight value. **The sediment Food Dilution and Tissue Translocation RQ/HC5 figures in this report are illustrative/non-quantitative and are excluded from the headline risk characterization (Sections 14-15) pending a genuine dry-weight sediment concentration.**

```{r sed-hazard-threshold-plot}
ggsave(sed_hazard_threshold_plot, filename = "figures/sed_hazard_threshold_plot.png", width = 9, height = 6, dpi = 300)
sed_hazard_threshold_plot
```

## 11.5 SPEC 1e: Sediment as a time-dependent, accumulating compartment

**Rationale.** Sediment is an accumulating, long-residence depositional compartment, and it is the sink for the large/dense particles that differential settling removes from the water column (Hoffman et al. 2026; the critical-size capture-fraction diagnostic in Section 13 quantifies that filtering mechanism for this dataset). Those deposited particles continue to fragment in situ, so — per [Thuy-Dung, Groenenberg & Koelmans (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1186/s43591-026-00210-8) — both exposure (bioaccessible particle number) and hazard (HC5, via which benthic species are size-accessible) are dynamic rather than static. A single-time-point sediment RQ is therefore a snapshot that can under-represent future risk in an accumulating bed. Everything in this section is a framework upgrade, not a live risk calculation: the sediment exposure concentration remains non-quantitative (`sediment_concentration_is_quantitative` = `r sediment_concentration_is_quantitative`, SPEC 1d), so nothing here re-introduces sediment into the headline risk conclusion (Sections 11.3.0/11.4.0/15.3).

### 11.5.1 SPEC 1e-i: Temporal fragmentation framing

- **Sediment is treated as a time-dependent, accumulating compartment.** Deposited microplastics continue to fragment, shifting the particle-size distribution toward smaller, more numerous, more bioaccessible particles over residence time in the bed.
- **Consequently, any static sediment metric is a lower-bound snapshot.** Both HC5 (which benthic species are size-accessible) and bioaccessible exposure evolve as fragmentation proceeds — the single-time-point Food Dilution/Tissue Translocation figures in Section 11.4 describe the sediment PSD's condition at the time of sampling, not its trajectory.
- **This compounds, rather than substitutes for, the SPEC 1d exposure-concentration problem.** Even once a genuine dry-weight sediment concentration becomes available, a single power-law fit to that concentration would still understate risk relative to the bed's future, more-fragmented state.
- Cite [Thuy-Dung, Groenenberg & Koelmans (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1186/s43591-026-00210-8) — a prospective, temporally-explicit risk framework for fragmenting microplastics (size-independent fragmentation rate constant *k*~frag~, doubling time *T*~D~) in which HC5 and RCR are time-dependent because shrinking particles become bioaccessible to progressively more sensitive species; the source paper's median HC5 example drops from 2.1×10⁴ to 1.95×10³ particles/kg when a sensitive species becomes accessible, and individual-species RCR>1 can precede a derivable community SSD by roughly a decade. Cross-reference: the Hoffman et al. (2026) differential-settling sink argument already used in this document (Section 13's critical-size diagnostic) is the mechanism that puts large/dense particles into the sediment bed in the first place; SPEC 1e is about what happens to them *after* they arrive.

### 11.5.3 SPEC 1e-iii: Time-varying bioaccessibility (documented; future enhancement)

Making the existing pSSD++ bioaccessibility size-gate explicitly time-dependent (HC5(*t*)/RCR(*t*) as a trajectory) is deferred: it needs a residence-time/age-of-deposition axis that does not exist in the source sediment dataset. Full scoping in Appendix C.

### 11.5.4 SPEC 1e-iv: Most-sensitive-species screen (sediment)

Per Thuy-Dung et al. (2026), individual-species risk can precede a derivable community SSD signal by roughly a decade, and the sediment benthic SSD here is small and comparatively unstable (`r nrow(tox_data_sed)` records, `r dplyr::n_distinct(tox_data_sed$Species)` species). This screen identifies the single most sensitive species (lowest aligned effect dose) per ERM and reports it alongside the community HC5 already computed in Section 11.4 — as an early-warning companion, not a replacement.

```{r sediment-most-sensitive-species}
mss_sed <- most_sensitive_species(erm_registry_sed, dose_col = "dose_new_particles_kg")

knitr::kable(
  mss_sed,
  digits = 3,
  caption = paste0(
    "SPEC 1e-iv: most-sensitive-species screen, sediment benthic dataset (n = ", nrow(tox_data_sed),
    " records, ", dplyr::n_distinct(tox_data_sed$Species), " species). median_EC (particles/kg dw) is the ",
    "most-sensitive species' own median aligned dose -- an early-warning companion to, not a replacement for, ",
    "the community HC5 in Section 11.4."
  )
)

mss_sed_fd <- dplyr::filter(mss_sed, ERM == "Food Dilution")
mss_sed_tt <- dplyr::filter(mss_sed, ERM == "Tissue Translocation")
```

For Food Dilution, the single most sensitive species among the `r mss_sed_fd$n_species` sediment benthic species considered is *`r mss_sed_fd$Species`* (median aligned dose = `r signif(mss_sed_fd$median_EC, 3)` particles/kg dw, `r mss_sed_fd$n_records` aligned records), compared with the community Food Dilution HC5 of `r signif(sed_HC5_food_dilution_pkg, 3)` particles/kg dw computed in Section 11.4. For Tissue Translocation, the most sensitive species is *`r mss_sed_tt$Species`* (median aligned dose = `r signif(mss_sed_tt$median_EC, 3)` particles/kg dw, `r mss_sed_tt$n_records` records), compared with the community Tissue Translocation HC5 of `r signif(sed_HC5_tissue_translocation_pkg, 3)` particles/kg dw. As Section 11.5.3 notes, a finer PSD from continued fragmentation could bring additional, potentially more sensitive species into bioaccessible range over time, which is part of why this individual-species screen is worth tracking alongside the community HC5 rather than assuming the current community SSD is stable. **This screen does not change the sediment exclusion from the headline conclusion** (its inputs are the same non-quantitative-exposure sediment pathway); the companion individual-species screen for the quantitative river/ocean water compartments is reported in Section 15.4, once every matrix's hazard objects have been computed.

---

# 12. Ocean Water

Ocean water samples were collected from the coastal/marine environment and analyzed using the same µFTIR workflow as river water. Marine species are evaluated using the PSSDplusplus marine toxicity endpoints and alignment parameters, which characterize exposure and hazard in particles/L rather than particles/kg (sediment).

## 12.1 Particle data and C-PSD fitting

### Particle volume computation

```{r ocean-volume}
# Compute W/L thickness ratio from ocean particles (same instrument as river)
ratio_tbl_ocean <- raw_particles_ocean |>
  dplyr::mutate(WL = 1 / aspect_ratio) |>
  dplyr::group_by(shape) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    n      = dplyr::n(),
    r_med  = median(WL, na.rm = TRUE),
    r_low  = quantile(WL, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    r_high = quantile(WL, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

raw_particles_ocean <- raw_particles_ocean |>
  assign_polymer_density(lookup = polymer_density_tbl) |>
  dplyr::left_join(ratio_tbl_ocean |> dplyr::select(shape, r_med), by = "shape") |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    height_um = r_med * width_um,
    V_um3 = dplyr::case_when(
      shape == "fragment" ~ (pi / 6) * length_um * width_um * height_um,
      shape == "fiber"    ~ pi * (width_um / 2)^2 * length_um,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_
    ),
    mass_ug = V_um3 * density_g_cm3,
    mass_ug_fixed_density_1.1 = V_um3 * 1.1
  )

cat("Ocean particles: n =", nrow(raw_particles_ocean),
    "| shapes:", paste(sort(unique(raw_particles_ocean$shape)), collapse = ", "), "\n")
```

### Particle length

```{r cpsd-fits-ocean-length}
cpsd_fits_ocean_length <- fit_cpsd_by_shape(
  raw_particles_ocean, value_col = "length_um",
  config = list(
    fragment = list(bin_um = 5, fit_range_um = c(NA_real_, NA_real_)),
    fiber    = list(bin_um = 5, fit_range_um = c(NA_real_, NA_real_)),
    all      = list(bin_um = 5, fit_range_um = c(NA_real_, NA_real_))
  )
)
cpsd_fit_ocean_frag  <- cpsd_fits_ocean_length$fragment
cpsd_fit_ocean_fiber <- cpsd_fits_ocean_length$fiber
cpsd_fit_ocean_all   <- cpsd_fits_ocean_length$all

set.seed(8003)
alpha_ocean    <- alpha_dist(mu = cpsd_fit_ocean_all$a_psd, sd = cpsd_fit_ocean_all$se_a_psd, n = n_mc, structural_sd = slope_structural_sd)
alpha_ocean_mu <- mean(alpha_ocean)
alpha_ocean_se <- sd(alpha_ocean)

cat("Ocean All: alpha =", signif(cpsd_fit_ocean_all$a_cpsd, 2), "±",
    signif(cpsd_fit_ocean_all$se_a_cpsd, 2),
    "| LOD =", signif(cpsd_fit_ocean_all$lower_lod_used_um, 2), "–",
    signif(cpsd_fit_ocean_all$upper_lod_um, 2), "µm\n")
```

#### Plots

```{r}
ocean_length_fits <- list(fragment = cpsd_fit_ocean_frag, fiber = cpsd_fit_ocean_fiber, all = cpsd_fit_ocean_all)
ocean_length_fits <- ocean_length_fits[names(MP_PALETTE)[names(MP_PALETTE) %in% names(ocean_length_fits)]]

ocean_length_cpsd_plot <- plot_cpsd_multi(ocean_length_fits, title = "Ocean water C-PSD fits by shape", attribute = "Length")
ggsave(ocean_length_cpsd_plot, filename = "figures/ocean_length_cpsd_plot.png", width = 8, height = 6, dpi = 300)
ocean_length_cpsd_plot
```

### Particle surface area

```{r cpsd-fits-ocean-area}
cpsd_fits_ocean_area <- fit_cpsd_by_shape(
  raw_particles_ocean, value_col = "area_um2",
  config = list(
    fragment = list(bin_um = 500, fit_range_um = c(2000, 50000)),
    fiber    = list(bin_um = 500, fit_range_um = c(2000, 500000)),
    all      = list(bin_um = 500, fit_range_um = c(2000, 500000))
  )
)
cpsd_fit_area_ocean_frag  <- cpsd_fits_ocean_area$fragment
cpsd_fit_area_ocean_fiber <- cpsd_fits_ocean_area$fiber
cpsd_fit_area_ocean       <- cpsd_fits_ocean_area$all

cat("Ocean All SA: alpha =", signif(cpsd_fit_area_ocean$a_cpsd, 2), "±",
    signif(cpsd_fit_area_ocean$se_a_cpsd, 2),
    "| LOD =", signif(cpsd_fit_area_ocean$lower_lod_used_um, 2), "–",
    signif(cpsd_fit_area_ocean$upper_lod_um, 2), "µm²\n")
```

#### Plots

```{r ocean-area-cpsd-plot}
ocean_area_fits <- list(fragment = cpsd_fit_area_ocean_frag, fiber = cpsd_fit_area_ocean_fiber, all = cpsd_fit_area_ocean)
ocean_area_cpsd_plot <- plot_cpsd_multi(ocean_area_fits, title = "Ocean water C-PSD fits by shape", attribute = "Area")
ggsave(ocean_area_cpsd_plot, filename = "figures/ocean_surfacearea_cpsd_plot.png", width = 8, height = 6, dpi = 300)
ocean_area_cpsd_plot
```

### Particle volume

Note: ocean's fragment volume fit uses the same length/width-consistent
`volume_lod_bounds()` approach as river and sediment (Section 4.2.3). Its **fiber** fit does
not: ocean has only `r sum(raw_particles_ocean$shape == "fiber")` fiber particles total, and
even the corrected (length/width-consistent, not isotropic) fiber volume-LOD window contains
just 4 of them — too few to constrain a fit. Ocean's fiber volume fit instead falls back to
the Segur algorithm's own auto-detected LOD window. Similarly, the "all" (pooled shapes) fit
uses the **fragment-only** volume-LOD window rather than the fragment/fiber union: with only
`r sum(raw_particles_ocean$shape == "fiber")` fibers, the union window is dominated by a
handful of sparse, noisy fiber-derived bounds and destabilizes the pooled fit (fragments
outnumber fibers roughly 10:1 in this matrix, so anchoring "all" to fragment's reliable range
is the more defensible choice here).

```{r ocean-volume-lod-bounds}
r_med_frag_ocean  <- ratio_tbl_ocean$r_med[ratio_tbl_ocean$shape == "fragment"]
r_med_fiber_ocean <- ratio_tbl_ocean$r_med[ratio_tbl_ocean$shape == "fiber"]
vlb_ocean <- volume_lod_bounds(cpsd_fit_ocean_frag, cpsd_fit_ocean_fiber, r_med_frag_ocean, r_med_fiber_ocean)
cat("Ocean fragment volume LOD: [", signif(vlb_ocean$fragment[1], 2), ",", signif(vlb_ocean$fragment[2], 2), "] µm³\n")
cat("Ocean fiber    volume LOD (informational only — too few particles to use as a fit constraint): [",
    signif(vlb_ocean$fiber[1], 2), ",", signif(vlb_ocean$fiber[2], 2), "] µm³\n")
```

```{r cpsd-fits-ocean-volume}
# fragment and all use the same uniform vol_bin_um as river/sediment. fiber is the one
# documented exception (see note above): with only 4 particles inside its physically-
# derived window, no fixed window is viable, so it falls back to auto-detection
# (fit_range_um = NA) with a coarser bin width appropriate to its much wider absolute
# volume range (up to ~3e7 µm³, vs ~7e5 µm³ for fragment) — fine bins there would be
# almost entirely empty regardless of methodology, per the small-sample diagnosis above.
ocean_fiber_vol_bin_um <- 1e6
cpsd_fits_ocean_volume <- fit_cpsd_by_shape(
  raw_particles_ocean, value_col = "V_um3",
  config = list(
    fragment = list(bin_um = vol_bin_um,          fit_range_um = vlb_ocean$fragment),
    fiber    = list(bin_um = ocean_fiber_vol_bin_um, fit_range_um = c(NA_real_, NA_real_)),
    all      = list(bin_um = vol_bin_um,          fit_range_um = vlb_ocean$fragment)
  )
)
cpsd_fit_volume_ocean_frag  <- cpsd_fits_ocean_volume$fragment
cpsd_fit_volume_ocean_fiber <- cpsd_fits_ocean_volume$fiber
cpsd_fit_volume_ocean       <- cpsd_fits_ocean_volume$all

cat("Ocean All Volume: alpha =", signif(cpsd_fit_volume_ocean$a_cpsd, 2), "±",
    signif(cpsd_fit_volume_ocean$se_a_cpsd, 2),
    "| LOD =", signif(cpsd_fit_volume_ocean$lower_lod_used_um, 2), "–",
    signif(cpsd_fit_volume_ocean$upper_lod_um, 2), "µm³\n")
```

#### Plots

```{r}
ocean_volume_fits <- list(fragment = cpsd_fit_volume_ocean_frag, fiber = cpsd_fit_volume_ocean_fiber, all = cpsd_fit_volume_ocean)
ocean_volume_cpsd_plot <- plot_cpsd_multi(ocean_volume_fits, title = "Ocean water C-PSD fits by shape", attribute = "Volume")
ggsave(ocean_volume_cpsd_plot, filename = "figures/ocean_volume_cpsd_plot.png", width = 8, height = 6, dpi = 300)
ocean_volume_cpsd_plot
```

## 12.1.1 All-matrix particle-length PSD comparison with MPSizeBase

This section is intentionally placed after the river, sediment, and ocean length C-PSDs have all been calculated. It imports Segur et al.'s MPSizeBase workbook directly from `assets/SI/SI 3 code and data/MPsizeBase_v15_05_2026.xlsx`, reads the workbook `Read Me`, and parses one literature *a*~psd~ value per `PSD_ID` from the `Literature PSD data` tab. The `cumsum_powerlaw_alpha` column is already the converted BN-PSD/differential slope (*a*~psd~ = *a*~cpsd~ - 1), so no additional conversion is applied.

```{r alpha-comparison-all-matrices-mpsizebase, fig.width=12, fig.height=7, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
mpsizebase_path <- file.path(
  proj_root, "assets", "SI", "SI 3 code and data", "MPsizeBase_v15_05_2026.xlsx"
)

mpsizebase_readme <- readxl::read_excel(
  mpsizebase_path,
  sheet = "Read Me",
  col_names = FALSE
) |>
  dplyr::filter(dplyr::if_any(dplyr::everything(), ~ !is.na(.x)))

knitr::kable(
  mpsizebase_readme,
  caption = "MPSizeBase workbook Read Me sheet"
)

mpsizebase_literature_raw <- readxl::read_excel(
  mpsizebase_path,
  sheet = "Literature PSD data",
  skip = 2,
  .name_repair = "unique"
)

required_mpsizebase_cols <- c(
  "PSD_ID", "Study", "Year", "Ocean", "Sample_type", "MP_shape",
  "Low_size", "High_size", "cumsum_slope", "cumsum_powerlaw_alpha"
)
missing_mpsizebase_cols <- setdiff(required_mpsizebase_cols, names(mpsizebase_literature_raw))
if (length(missing_mpsizebase_cols) > 0) {
  stop("MPSizeBase Literature PSD data sheet is missing columns: ",
       paste(missing_mpsizebase_cols, collapse = ", "))
}

literature_psd_alpha <- mpsizebase_literature_raw |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(PSD_ID), !is.na(cumsum_powerlaw_alpha)) |>
  dplyr::group_by(PSD_ID) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    Study = dplyr::first(Study),
    Year = dplyr::first(Year),
    Literature_matrix = dplyr::first(Sample_type),
    Ocean_or_region = dplyr::first(Ocean),
    Shape = dplyr::case_when(
      grepl("fiber", dplyr::first(MP_shape), ignore.case = TRUE) ~ "fiber",
      grepl("fragment", dplyr::first(MP_shape), ignore.case = TRUE) ~ "fragment",
      TRUE ~ as.character(dplyr::first(MP_shape))
    ),
    n_bins = dplyr::n(),
    a_cpsd = dplyr::first(as.numeric(cumsum_slope)),
    a_psd = dplyr::first(as.numeric(cumsum_powerlaw_alpha)),
    lod_low_um = suppressWarnings(min(as.numeric(Low_size), na.rm = TRUE)),
    lod_high_um = suppressWarnings(max(as.numeric(High_size), na.rm = TRUE)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    Source = "Segur et al. MPSizeBase",
    Matrix = dplyr::case_when(
      Literature_matrix == "Ocean" ~ "Literature ocean",
      Literature_matrix == "Atmosphere" ~ "Literature atmosphere",
      TRUE ~ paste("Literature", Literature_matrix)
    ),
    alpha_abs = abs(a_psd),
    label = PSD_ID
  )

fit_to_alpha_row <- function(matrix_label, shape_label, fit, psd_id, source_detail) {
  tibble::tibble(
    PSD_ID = psd_id,
    Study = "This study",
    Year = NA_real_,
    Source = source_detail,
    Matrix = matrix_label,
    Shape = shape_label,
    n_bins = fit$n_bins,
    a_cpsd = fit$a_cpsd,
    a_psd = fit$a_psd,
    lod_low_um = fit$lower_lod_used_um,
    lod_high_um = fit$upper_lod_um,
    alpha_abs = abs(fit$a_psd),
    label = psd_id
  )
}

this_study_length_alpha <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  fit_to_alpha_row("River water", "all", cpsd_fit_all, "W2W_river_all", "This study matrix/shape"),
  fit_to_alpha_row("River water", "fragment", cpsd_fit_frag, "W2W_river_fragment", "This study matrix/shape"),
  fit_to_alpha_row("River water", "fiber", cpsd_fit_fiber, "W2W_river_fiber", "This study matrix/shape"),
  fit_to_alpha_row("Sediment", "all", cpsd_fit_sed_all, "W2W_sediment_all", "This study matrix/shape"),
  fit_to_alpha_row("Sediment", "fragment", cpsd_fit_sed_frag, "W2W_sediment_fragment", "This study matrix/shape"),
  fit_to_alpha_row("Sediment", "fiber", cpsd_fit_sed_fiber, "W2W_sediment_fiber", "This study matrix/shape"),
  fit_to_alpha_row("Ocean water", "all", cpsd_fit_ocean_all, "W2W_ocean_all", "This study matrix/shape"),
  fit_to_alpha_row("Ocean water", "fragment", cpsd_fit_ocean_frag, "W2W_ocean_fragment", "This study matrix/shape"),
  fit_to_alpha_row("Ocean water", "fiber", cpsd_fit_ocean_fiber, "W2W_ocean_fiber", "This study matrix/shape"),
  loc_summary |>
    dplyr::transmute(
      PSD_ID = paste0("W2W_river_site_", gsub("[^A-Za-z0-9]+", "_", location)),
      Study = "This study",
      Year = NA_real_,
      Source = "This study river site",
      Matrix = "River water",
      Shape = "all-site",
      n_bins = n_bins,
      a_cpsd = a_cpsd,
      a_psd = a_psd,
      lod_low_um = lod_low_um,
      lod_high_um = lod_high_um,
      alpha_abs = abs(a_psd),
      label = location
    )
)

## Freshwater/marine-only comparison, extended with Wang/Zhao/Kooi literature
##
## Per revision: literature "atmosphere" values are dropped (not a useful
## comparator for aquatic matrices), as is the sediment matrix (neither
## freshwater nor marine surface water). This study is split into its own
## River (freshwater) and Ocean (marine) rows, each retaining the
## fragment/fiber/all shape distinction and this-study point labels. Three
## additional literature sources reported in Section 4.2.1.2 are added:
## Wang et al. (2026), Segur et al. (2026) ocean reference, and Kooi et al.
## (2021) freshwater/marine defaults, plus Zhao et al. (2026). Zhao's
## meta-analysis only reports a pooled mean +/- SD across 45 studies (no
## per-study values, no fragment/fiber split, and the underlying studies mix
## freshwater and marine sites) -- it is therefore plotted as a single
## point +/- SD, shape "all", in an "unclassified" matrix color rather than
## forced into freshwater or marine.

literature_ocean_only <- literature_psd_alpha |>
  dplyr::filter(Matrix == "Literature ocean")

dropped_literature_matrix <- literature_psd_alpha |>
  dplyr::filter(Matrix != "Literature ocean") |>
  dplyr::count(Matrix, name = "n_PSD_IDs")
if (nrow(dropped_literature_matrix) > 0) {
  cat("MPSizeBase literature PSD_IDs excluded from the freshwater/marine comparison ",
      "(not ocean, e.g. atmosphere):\n", sep = "")
  print(dropped_literature_matrix)
}

# Deterministic within-row x offsets (added at source, not recomputed from a
# shared group size later) so fragment/fiber/all never collide with the
# per-site cluster regardless of how many river sites there are.
shape_offset <- function(shape) dplyr::case_when(
  shape == "fragment" ~ -0.15,
  shape == "fiber"    ~  0.15,
  TRUE                ~  0
)

this_study_river_shape <- this_study_length_alpha |>
  dplyr::filter(Matrix == "River water") |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    Source = "This study — River (freshwater)",
    Matrix = "Freshwater",
    Shape,
    alpha_abs,
    se = NA_real_,
    point_label = Shape,
    n_desc = paste0(n_bins, " length bins (C-PSD fit)"),
    lod_desc = paste0(round(lod_low_um), "–", round(lod_high_um), " µm (Segur LOD)"),
    offset = shape_offset(Shape)
  )

this_study_ocean_shape <- this_study_length_alpha |>
  dplyr::filter(Matrix == "Ocean water") |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    Source = "This study — Ocean (marine)",
    Matrix = "Marine",
    Shape,
    alpha_abs,
    se = NA_real_,
    point_label = Shape,
    n_desc = paste0(n_bins, " length bins (C-PSD fit)"),
    lod_desc = paste0(round(lod_low_um), "–", round(lod_high_um), " µm (Segur LOD)"),
    offset = shape_offset(Shape)
  )

# Per-site points sit in their own band (0.30-0.30+0.02*(n-1)) above the
# fragment/fiber/all cluster (-0.15 to 0.15), so they never overlap it.
this_study_river_sites <- loc_summary |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    Source = "This study — River (freshwater)",
    Matrix = "Freshwater",
    Shape = "all-site",
    alpha_abs = abs(a_psd),
    se = NA_real_,
    point_label = location,
    n_desc = paste0(n_bins, " length bins (C-PSD fit)"),
    lod_desc = paste0(round(lod_low_um), "–", round(lod_high_um), " µm (Segur LOD)"),
    offset = 0.30 + 0.02 * (dplyr::row_number() - 1)
  )

# Wang et al. (2026): actual per-site fits (Talanta 296, 128417, sec. 3.1.2).
# Combined n = 6 samples (2 Eijsden + 4 Lobith); Lobith n = 4; Eijsden n = 2.
# SD values are the reported fit SDs, used here as the plotted error bar.
wang_df <- tibble::tibble(
  Source      = "Wang et al. 2026 — Rhine/Meuse rivers (freshwater, µFTIR)",
  Matrix      = "Freshwater",
  Shape       = "all",
  alpha_abs   = c(3.65, 3.89, 3.19),
  se          = c(0.21, 0.36, 0.58),
  point_label = c("Combined", "Lobith (Rhine)", "Eijsden (Meuse)"),
  n_desc      = c("n = 6 samples (pooled fit)", "n = 4 samples (site mean)", "n = 2 samples (site mean)"),
  lod_desc    = c("118 µm (min, pooled fit)", "38–92 µm (per-sample range)", "35–90 µm (per-sample range)"),
  offset      = c(-0.2, 0, 0.2)
)

segur_ocean_ref_df <- tibble::tibble(
  Source      = "Segur et al. 2026 — ocean reference (marine, C-PSD)",
  Matrix      = "Marine",
  Shape       = "all",
  alpha_abs   = 2.66,
  se          = NA_real_,
  point_label = NA_character_,
  n_desc      = "Reference default (not sample-based)",
  lod_desc    = "Not reported",
  offset      = 0
)

kooi_df <- tibble::tibble(
  Source      = c("Kooi et al. 2021 — freshwater default", "Kooi et al. 2021 — marine default"),
  Matrix      = c("Freshwater", "Marine"),
  Shape       = "all",
  alpha_abs   = c(kooi_alpha_freshwater, kooi_alpha_marine),
  se          = c(PSSDplusplus::param_default_values$alpha.freshwater.sd,
                   PSSDplusplus::param_default_values$alpha.marine.sd),
  point_label = NA_character_,
  n_desc      = "PSSDplusplus::param_default_values literature synthesis default",
  lod_desc    = "Not reported",
  offset      = 0
)

# Zhao et al. (2026): only a pooled mean +/- SD across 45 studies is reported
# (Fig. 4a); no per-study values, no fragment/fiber split, freshwater/marine
# not separated in source. Plotted as point + SD (not a boxplot) per Zhao's
# own reporting, with an unclassified "mixed" matrix color.
zhao_df <- tibble::tibble(
  Source      = "Zhao et al. 2026 — global surface water (mixed F+M, unclassified)",
  Matrix      = "Mixed (unclassified)",
  Shape       = "all",
  alpha_abs   = c(1.50, 1.53),
  se          = c(0.53, NA_real_),
  point_label = c("Raw (unadjusted)", "Mesh-adjusted"),
  n_desc      = "n = 45 studies (meta-analysis; freshwater + marine pooled, not separated in source)",
  lod_desc    = "10–5000 µm (model domain)",
  offset      = c(-0.15, 0.15)
)

literature_ocean_df <- literature_ocean_only |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    Source      = "Literature ocean (MPSizeBase compilation, marine)",
    Matrix      = "Marine",
    Shape       = "all",
    alpha_abs,
    se          = NA_real_,
    point_label = NA_character_,
    n_desc      = paste0("PSD_ID = ", PSD_ID),
    lod_desc    = paste0(round(lod_low_um), "–", round(lod_high_um), " µm"),
    offset      = 0
  )

source_levels_bottom_to_top <- c(
  "Zhao et al. 2026 — global surface water (mixed F+M, unclassified)",
  "Kooi et al. 2021 — marine default",
  "Segur et al. 2026 — ocean reference (marine, C-PSD)",
  "Literature ocean (MPSizeBase compilation, marine)",
  "This study — Ocean (marine)",
  "Kooi et al. 2021 — freshwater default",
  "Wang et al. 2026 — Rhine/Meuse rivers (freshwater, µFTIR)",
  "This study — River (freshwater)"
)

alpha_forest_df <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  this_study_river_shape, this_study_river_sites, this_study_ocean_shape,
  wang_df, segur_ocean_ref_df, kooi_df, literature_ocean_df, zhao_df
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    Source     = factor(Source, levels = source_levels_bottom_to_top),
    Matrix     = factor(Matrix, levels = c("Freshwater", "Marine", "Mixed (unclassified)")),
    Shape      = factor(Shape, levels = c("fragment", "fiber", "all", "all-site")),
    is_this_study   = grepl("^This study", Source),
    is_boxplot_row  = Source == "Literature ocean (MPSizeBase compilation, marine)",
    # offset was fixed at each source-piece's own construction (above), so it
    # is never recomputed from a mismatched/shared group size here.
    x_pos = as.numeric(Source) + offset
  )

matrix_pal_forest <- c(
  "Freshwater"            = "#0072B2",
  "Marine"                = "#009E73",
  "Mixed (unclassified)"  = "#999999"
)
shape_pal_forest <- c(fragment = 16, fiber = 17, all = 15, "all-site" = 1)


alpha_comparison_plot <- ggplot2::ggplot(
  alpha_forest_df,
  ggplot2::aes(x = x_pos, y = alpha_abs)
) +
  ggplot2::geom_boxplot(
    data = alpha_forest_df |> dplyr::filter(is_boxplot_row),
    ggplot2::aes(group = Source, fill = Matrix),
    color = "#009E73", alpha = 0.12, width = 0.55, outlier.shape = NA
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_errorbar(
    data = alpha_forest_df |> dplyr::filter(!is.na(se)),
    ggplot2::aes(ymin = alpha_abs - se, ymax = alpha_abs + se, color = Matrix),
    width = 0.10, linewidth = 0.6
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_jitter(
    data = alpha_forest_df |> dplyr::filter(is_boxplot_row),
    ggplot2::aes(color = Matrix, shape = Shape),
    width = 0.16, height = 0, alpha = 0.35, size = 1.6
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(
    data = alpha_forest_df |> dplyr::filter(!is_boxplot_row),
    ggplot2::aes(color = Matrix, shape = Shape),
    size = 3.2, alpha = 0.95
  ) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(
    data = alpha_forest_df |> dplyr::filter(is_this_study, !is.na(point_label)),
    ggplot2::aes(label = point_label),
    size = 3.0, max.overlaps = Inf, show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_color_manual(values = matrix_pal_forest, drop = FALSE, name = "Matrix") +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = matrix_pal_forest, drop = FALSE, guide = "none") +
  ggplot2::scale_shape_manual(values = shape_pal_forest, name = "Shape", drop = FALSE) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq_along(source_levels_bottom_to_top),
    labels = stringr::str_wrap(source_levels_bottom_to_top, width = 40),
    expand = ggplot2::expansion(add = 0.6)
  ) +
  ggplot2::coord_flip() +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = expression("|" * italic(a)[psd] * "| from particle-length PSD"),
    color = "Matrix",
    shape = "Shape",
    title = "Freshwater and marine particle-length PSD slopes: this study vs. literature",
    subtitle = paste(
      "Sediment and literature-atmosphere values excluded (not freshwater/marine surface water).",
      "This study is split into River (freshwater) and Ocean (marine) rows, each retaining the fragment/fiber/all shape distinction.",
      sep = "\n"
    ),
    caption = paste0(
      "Colors match freshwater/marine usage elsewhere in this document (blue = freshwater, green = marine). ",
      "Zhao et al. (2026) is unclassified gray because its 45-study meta-analysis pools freshwater and marine sites ",
      "and reports only a pooled mean ± SD (no per-study values or shape split), plotted as point ± SD rather than a boxplot. ",
      "Literature ocean (MPSizeBase) box+jitter uses ", nrow(literature_ocean_only), " individual PSD_IDs. ",
      "Wang et al. (2026) SDs are the reported per-fit SDs (Talanta 296, 128417)."
    )
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 16) +
  ggplot2::theme(
    axis.text.y = ggplot2::element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "right",
    panel.border = ggplot2::element_rect(color = "gray82", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.4),
    plot.title = ggplot2::element_text(size = 15),
    plot.subtitle = ggplot2::element_text(size = 10.5, color = "gray30"),
    plot.caption = ggplot2::element_text(size = 8, color = "gray45", hjust = 0)
  )


ggsave(alpha_comparison_plot, filename = "figures/alpha_comparison_plot.png", width = 14, height = 8, dpi = 300)
alpha_comparison_plot

knitr::kable(
  alpha_forest_df |>
    dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(as.numeric(Source))) |>
    dplyr::transmute(
      Dataset       = as.character(Source),
      Matrix        = as.character(Matrix),
      Shape         = as.character(Shape),
      Point         = dplyr::coalesce(point_label, "(summary)"),
      `|a_psd|`     = round(alpha_abs, 3),
      SE            = ifelse(is.na(se), "—", as.character(round(se, 3))),
      n             = n_desc,
      `LOD (µm)` = lod_desc
    ),
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Metadata (n, LOD, matrix) for every point in figures/alpha_comparison_plot.png, ordered top-to-bottom as plotted."
)

knitr::kable(
  this_study_length_alpha |>
    dplyr::select(Source, Matrix, Shape, PSD_ID, a_cpsd, a_psd, lod_low_um, lod_high_um, n_bins),
  digits = 3,
  caption = "All this-study particle-length PSD slopes (river, sediment, ocean) computed in this document; the freshwater/marine subset is plotted in figures/alpha_comparison_plot.png"
)
```

## 12.3 Marine toxicity data

```{r ocean-tox-data}
tox_data_ocean <- tomex2 |>
  dplyr::filter(
    env_f            == "Marine",
    Group            != "Bacterium",
    Group            != "Plant",
    effect.metric    != "HONEC",
    tier_zero_tech_f == "Red Criteria Passed",
    tier_zero_risk_f == "Red Criteria Passed",
    risk.13          != 0
  )

cat("Marine tox endpoints:", nrow(tox_data_ocean), "records,",
    length(unique(tox_data_ocean$Group)), "taxonomic groups\n")
```

### Parameter distributions

```{r ocean-aspect-ratio}
set.seed(9003)
R.ave_ocean_result <- bootstrap_aspect_ratio(raw_particles_ocean$aspect_ratio, n_boot = n_boot)
R.ave_ocean_vals   <- R.ave_ocean_result$vals
R.ave_ocean_mean   <- R.ave_ocean_result$boot_mean
R.ave_ocean_sd     <- R.ave_ocean_result$boot_sd

param_values_ocean <- PSSDplusplus::param_default_values

param_values_ocean[["alpha.marine"]]          <- -alpha_ocean_mu
param_values_ocean[["alpha.marine.sd"]]       <- alpha_ocean_se
param_values_ocean[["R.ave.water.marine"]]    <- R.ave_ocean_mean
param_values_ocean[["R.ave.water.marine.sd"]] <- R.ave_ocean_sd
# SPEC 1b: use the differential a_psd = a_cpsd - 1, not the cumulative a_cpsd
# (the cumulative value is 1.0 too shallow; see river/sediment blocks above).
param_values_ocean[["a.sa.marine"]]           <- -cpsd_fit_area_ocean$a_psd
param_values_ocean[["a.sa.marine.sd"]]        <- cpsd_fit_area_ocean$se_a_psd
param_values_ocean[["a.v.marine"]]            <- -cpsd_fit_volume_ocean$a_psd
param_values_ocean[["a.v.marine.sd"]]         <- cpsd_fit_volume_ocean$se_a_psd
# a.m.marine: use volume slope as proxy (mass ∝ density × volume; constant density → same slope)
param_values_ocean[["a.m.marine"]]            <- -cpsd_fit_volume_ocean$a_psd
param_values_ocean[["a.m.marine.sd"]]         <- cpsd_fit_volume_ocean$se_a_psd
# Keep all remaining params from param_default_values (same pattern as river section)
# a.ssa.marine, p.ave.marine etc. retain their validated defaults
param_values_ocean

# SPEC 1b acceptance check: a.v and a.m must be mutually consistent
stopifnot(abs(param_values_ocean$a.v.marine - param_values_ocean$a.m.marine) < 0.3)
```

### Build and visualize parameter distributions

```{r ocean-param-matrix}
set.seed(7003)
param_matrix_ocean <- matrix_function(
  n    = n_boot,
  params = param_values_ocean,
  upper.tissue.truncation.limit = 500,
  x1M_set = 1,
  x2D_set = 5000,
  include_marine_surface_water     = TRUE,
  include_freshwater_surface_water = FALSE,
  include_marine_sediment          = FALSE,
  include_freshwater_sediment      = FALSE
)

ocean_R_col  <- rlang::sym("R.ave.water.marine")
ocean_HW_col <- rlang::sym("H_W_ratio.water.marine")

param_matrix_ocean <- param_matrix_ocean |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    !!ocean_R_col  := sample(R.ave_ocean_vals, size = dplyr::n(), replace = TRUE),
    !!ocean_HW_col := sample(R.ave_ocean_vals, size = dplyr::n(), replace = TRUE)
  )

tryCatch(
  {
    alpha_combined_plot_ocean <- parameter_histograms_function(param_matrix_ocean, compartments = c("Marine Surface Water"))$alpha_combined_plot
    alpha_combined_plot_ocean <- label_matrix(alpha_combined_plot_ocean, "Ocean water")
    ggsave(alpha_combined_plot_ocean, filename = "figures/alpha_combined_plot_ocean.png", width = 9, height = 6, dpi = 300)
    alpha_combined_plot_ocean
  },
  error = function(e) message("Parameter histogram skipped: ", conditionMessage(e))
)
```

### Align toxicity data

```{r ocean-mc-sim}
# run_pssd_pipeline() (sourced from R/mp_risk_utils.R) bundles MC_sim_align_parallel(),
# the ERM-specific results_df filtering, erm_registry construction, and make_all_pSSDs()
# into one step used identically across river/sediment/ocean.
ocean_pssd <- run_pssd_pipeline(
  tox_data     = tox_data_ocean,
  param_matrix = param_matrix_ocean,
  environments = c("Marine"),
  cache_suffix = "ocean",
  dose_unit    = "L",
  n_sim        = n_boot,
  num_cores    = parallel::detectCores() - 2,
  sim          = 30,
  cv_uf        = 0.5,
  rmore_method = "lognormal",
  seed         = 5003
)
MC_sim_df_ocean    <- ocean_pssd$MC_sim_df
erm_registry_ocean <- ocean_pssd$erm_registry
```

Hoffman et al. (2026) frame the observed PSD as a transport-filtered distribution. A simple diagnostic is the capture fraction *f*(*d*, δ) = 1 − exp(−*w*~s~(*d*)·δ / *K*) and the critical size where *w*~s~(*d*)·δ / *K* ≈ 1. The calculation below uses Stokes settling/rise speed with user-supplied `delta_m` = `r hoffman_delta_m` m and `K_m2_s` = `r hoffman_K_m2_s` m^2/s. These are assumptions, not measured site parameters, and should be replaced with field-specific values before a mechanistic transport correction is attempted.

```{r hoffman-critical-size-piecewise}
matrix_fit_tbl <- tibble::tibble(
  Matrix = c("River water", "Sediment", "Ocean water"),
  cpsd_fit = list(cpsd_fit_all, cpsd_fit_sed_all, cpsd_fit_ocean_all),
  median_density_g_cm3 = c(
    median(raw_particles_river$density_g_cm3, na.rm = TRUE),
    median(raw_particles_sed$density_g_cm3, na.rm = TRUE),
    median(raw_particles_ocean$density_g_cm3, na.rm = TRUE)
  ),
  water_density_g_cm3 = c(1.00, 1.00, 1.025)
)

critical_piecewise_tbl <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(seq_len(nrow(matrix_fit_tbl)), function(i) {
  fit_i <- matrix_fit_tbl$cpsd_fit[[i]]
  dc_i <- estimate_critical_size(
    delta_m = hoffman_delta_m,
    K_m2_s = hoffman_K_m2_s,
    density_g_cm3 = matrix_fit_tbl$median_density_g_cm3[i],
    water_density_g_cm3 = matrix_fit_tbl$water_density_g_cm3[i]
  )
  pw_i <- piecewise_cpsd_diagnostic(fit_i)
  tibble::tibble(
    Matrix = matrix_fit_tbl$Matrix[i],
    median_density_g_cm3 = matrix_fit_tbl$median_density_g_cm3[i],
    critical_size_um = dc_i,
    fit_lod_low_um = fit_i$lower_lod_used_um,
    fit_lod_high_um = fit_i$upper_lod_um,
    straddles_critical_size = is.finite(dc_i) && dc_i >= fit_i$lower_lod_used_um && dc_i <= fit_i$upper_lod_um,
    single_a_cpsd = fit_i$a_cpsd,
    single_a_psd = fit_i$a_psd,
    piecewise_break_um = pw_i$break_um,
    piecewise_low_a_cpsd = pw_i$slope_low,
    piecewise_high_a_cpsd = pw_i$slope_high,
    piecewise_delta_aic = pw_i$delta_aic
  )
}))

knitr::kable(
  critical_piecewise_tbl,
  digits = 3,
  caption = "SPEC 4 diagnostic: critical size and two-segment C-PSD fit by matrix"
)
```

The piecewise fits are diagnostic only. A fit window that straddles the assumed critical size is flagged because the fitted single slope may blend a transport-distorted fine-size regime with the coarser-size regime. Per Hoffman et al. (2026), future refinement should prioritize measured 3-D geometry and polymer density over increasingly elaborate settling equations; even precise-geometry settling models retain substantial residual error, so settling-based corrections should be treated as bias-level adjustments rather than high-precision concentration estimates.

## 13.3 SPEC 2b: Piecewise (dual-slope) PSD as a bounding exposure case

The production `correction_factor()` extrapolates a single fitted power-law slope from the measured LOD window down to the 1 um target floor. The two-segment diagnostic above (§13.2) shows the data themselves often prefer a shallower fine-size slope below a break point and a steeper coarse-size slope above it (river ΔAIC in the diagnostic table strongly favors the two-segment model; sediment likewise). Because the sub-floor extrapolation zone (1 um to the fitted LOD) can straddle or sit near that break — and because the fitted critical size `d_c` for river (~36 um) falls inside that 1-50 um extrapolation zone rather than inside the fit window itself — a single coarse slope may not be the right model to extrapolate through that zone. Independent evidence that single power laws mis-extrapolate to small, unmeasured sizes: in the St Louis Estuary, a single power law extrapolated to 1.3-12 particles/L for 5-5000 um while flow cytometry directly measured 600-1,600 particles/L in the same system ([Thomas et al. 2024](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.est.3c10776)), and [Segur et al. (2026)](https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-8524083/v1) find size-aligned 1-5000 um concentrations average ~600x higher than reported values based on single-slope extrapolation. Both are cited as **evidence that single-power-law extrapolation to small sizes is unreliable in general**, not as a validated correction for this dataset.

`correction_factor_piecewise()` (`R/mp_risk_utils.R`, SPEC 2b) implements the two-segment alternative: it integrates dN/dL = k*L^a using the fine-segment differential slope over [1, break_um] and the coarse-segment differential slope over [break_um, 5000], with the coarse segment's density scaled so the two segments meet exactly (are continuous) at `break_um`. The piecewise cumulative slopes from the §13.2 diagnostic are converted to the differential convention (a_psd = a_cpsd - 1) internally via `slope_convention = "cumulative"`, consistent with the SPEC 1c guard. **This is a labeled bounding sensitivity, not a replacement for the single-slope production CF** — the production exposure pipeline (Sections 5-6, 9-10, 12) is unchanged. The 1 um-LOD_low sub-window is unconstrained by data in *both* the single-slope and piecewise case; the piecewise result quantifies structural (model-form) uncertainty in how that unconstrained sub-window is extrapolated, which is not captured by the Gaussian `slope_structural_sd` already added to the fit-uncertainty propagation.

```{r spec2b-piecewise-cf}
piecewise_cf_row <- function(matrix_label, piecewise_row, L_meas_min, L_meas_max) {
  brk <- piecewise_row$piecewise_break_um
  s_lo <- piecewise_row$piecewise_low_a_cpsd
  s_hi <- piecewise_row$piecewise_high_a_cpsd
  if (!is.finite(brk) || !is.finite(s_lo) || !is.finite(s_hi)) {
    return(tibble::tibble(Matrix = matrix_label, break_um = NA_real_, cf_piecewise = NA_real_))
  }
  cf_pw <- correction_factor_piecewise(
    a_low = s_lo, a_high = s_hi, break_um = brk,
    L_meas_min = L_meas_min, L_meas_max = L_meas_max,
    L_tar_min = 1, L_tar_max = 5000,
    slope_convention = "cumulative"
  )
  tibble::tibble(Matrix = matrix_label, break_um = brk, cf_piecewise = cf_pw)
}

pw_river <- piecewise_cf_row("River water", dplyr::filter(critical_piecewise_tbl, Matrix == "River water"), L_meas_min_use, L_meas_max_use)
pw_sed   <- piecewise_cf_row("Sediment",    dplyr::filter(critical_piecewise_tbl, Matrix == "Sediment"),    L_meas_min_use_sed, L_meas_max_use_sed)
pw_ocean <- piecewise_cf_row("Ocean water", dplyr::filter(critical_piecewise_tbl, Matrix == "Ocean water"), L_meas_min_ocean, L_meas_max_ocean)

# Piecewise sensitivity is an exposure-only (CF/EED) effect: apply the single
# piecewise CF point estimate to the raw per-sample measured concentrations,
# then bootstrap the EED exactly as for the single-slope case. Hazard (haz*)
# is unchanged, so any RQ shift below is attributable to the piecewise CF alone.
set.seed(9401)
eed_boot_piecewise_river <- if (is.finite(pw_river$cf_piecewise)) {
  bootstrap_eed(monitoring$C_measured_pL * pw_river$cf_piecewise, n_boot = n_boot, probs = c(0.5, 0.95))
} else NULL
set.seed(9402)
eed_boot_piecewise_sed <- if (is.finite(pw_sed$cf_piecewise)) {
  bootstrap_eed(monitoring_sed$C_measured_pkg * pw_sed$cf_piecewise, n_boot = n_boot, probs = c(0.5, 0.95))
} else NULL
set.seed(9403)
eed_boot_piecewise_ocean <- if (is.finite(pw_ocean$cf_piecewise)) {
  bootstrap_eed(monitoring_ocean$C_measured_pL * pw_ocean$cf_piecewise, n_boot = n_boot, probs = c(0.5, 0.95))
} else NULL

set.seed(9411)
risk_summary_piecewise_river <- if (!is.null(eed_boot_piecewise_river)) {
  summarize_rq(draw_rq_mc1d(haz, eed_boot_piecewise_river$q50, n_risk = n_risk))
} else NULL
set.seed(9412)
risk_summary_piecewise_sed <- if (!is.null(eed_boot_piecewise_sed)) {
  summarize_rq(draw_rq_mc1d(haz_sed, eed_boot_piecewise_sed$q50, n_risk = n_risk_sed))
} else NULL
set.seed(9413)
risk_summary_piecewise_ocean <- if (!is.null(eed_boot_piecewise_ocean)) {
  summarize_rq(draw_rq_mc1d(haz_ocean, eed_boot_piecewise_ocean$q50, n_risk = n_risk_ocean))
} else NULL
```

```{r spec2b-bounding-table}
cf_bounding_tbl <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  tibble::tibble(Matrix = "River water", break_um = pw_river$break_um,
                 CF_single_slope_p50 = median(combined_cf), CF_piecewise = pw_river$cf_piecewise,
                 EED_single_slope_q50 = median(eed_boot$q50),
                 EED_piecewise_q50 = if (!is.null(eed_boot_piecewise_river)) median(eed_boot_piecewise_river$q50) else NA_real_),
  tibble::tibble(Matrix = "Sediment", break_um = pw_sed$break_um,
                 CF_single_slope_p50 = median(combined_cf_sed), CF_piecewise = pw_sed$cf_piecewise,
                 EED_single_slope_q50 = median(eed_boot_sed$q50),
                 EED_piecewise_q50 = if (!is.null(eed_boot_piecewise_sed)) median(eed_boot_piecewise_sed$q50) else NA_real_),
  tibble::tibble(Matrix = "Ocean water", break_um = pw_ocean$break_um,
                 CF_single_slope_p50 = median(combined_cf_ocean), CF_piecewise = pw_ocean$cf_piecewise,
                 EED_single_slope_q50 = median(eed_boot_ocean$q50),
                 EED_piecewise_q50 = if (!is.null(eed_boot_piecewise_ocean)) median(eed_boot_piecewise_ocean$q50) else NA_real_)
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(CF_ratio_piecewise_vs_single = CF_piecewise / CF_single_slope_p50)

knitr::kable(
  cf_bounding_tbl, digits = 3,
  caption = "SPEC 2b: single-slope (production) vs. piecewise (bounding sensitivity) correction factor and EED, by matrix"
)

rq_bounding_tbl <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  dplyr::mutate(risk_summary,                                     Matrix = "River water", Case = "Single-slope (production)"),
  if (!is.null(risk_summary_piecewise_river)) dplyr::mutate(risk_summary_piecewise_river, Matrix = "River water", Case = "Piecewise (bounding)"),
  dplyr::mutate(risk_summary_sed,                                 Matrix = "Sediment",    Case = "Single-slope (production)"),
  if (!is.null(risk_summary_piecewise_sed)) dplyr::mutate(risk_summary_piecewise_sed, Matrix = "Sediment",    Case = "Piecewise (bounding)"),
  dplyr::mutate(risk_summary_ocean,                               Matrix = "Ocean water", Case = "Single-slope (production)"),
  if (!is.null(risk_summary_piecewise_ocean)) dplyr::mutate(risk_summary_piecewise_ocean, Matrix = "Ocean water", Case = "Piecewise (bounding)")
) |>
  dplyr::filter(ERM %in% c("Food Dilution", "Tissue Translocation"), HCx == 5) |>
  dplyr::select(Matrix, Case, ERM, RQ_p50, RQ_p95, P_exceed) |>
  dplyr::arrange(Matrix, ERM, Case)

knitr::kable(
  rq_bounding_tbl, digits = 3,
  caption = "SPEC 2b: Food Dilution / Tissue Translocation HC5 RQ bounding range, single-slope (production) vs. piecewise (bounding sensitivity)"
)
```

**Bounding range interpretation.** The table above states, per matrix, the single-slope production RQ alongside the piecewise-sensitivity RQ; whichever is larger sets the upper bound of the sensitivity range and whichever is smaller sets the lower bound. Because the fine-size (sub-break) slope from the §13.2 diagnostic is shallower than the coarse-size slope for the matrices where the two-segment model is favored, the piecewise CF is expected to sit *below* the single-slope CF (less extrapolated mass assigned to the unconstrained 1 um-LOD_low zone) — i.e., the piecewise bound is expected to **narrow** the exposure (and therefore RQ) estimate relative to the single-slope production value, not widen it, for this dataset. This is stated as an expectation to be read against the rendered numbers above, not assumed; if a matrix's piecewise CF instead exceeds the single-slope CF, that reversal is itself informative about how sensitive the conclusion is to the extrapolation model and should be flagged rather than averaged away. Regardless of direction, the single-slope CF remains the production default per the guardrails in the corrective-revision spec; the piecewise result is reported here strictly as a labeled sensitivity bound. **Sediment caveat (SPEC 1d):** the Sediment column/row above is illustrative only, for the same reason noted in Section 13.1/11.3.0 — its exposure concentration is not a genuine particles/kg-dry-weight value.


# 14. Combined risk quotient comparison across matrices

`plot_rq_hist_combined()` (sourced from `R/risk_plotting.R`) row-binds the 1D Monte Carlo
risk quotient draws for all three matrices — now that river (Section 8), sediment
(Section 11.4), and ocean (Section 12.4) each have a 1D RQ distribution — into a single
figure faceted by **Matrix (rows) × ERM (columns)**, so every panel is self-labeled by
matrix rather than relying on a caption. **The Sediment row is retained here for completeness
but is illustrative/non-quantitative (SPEC 1d, Section 11.3.0/11.4.0): its exposure
concentration is not a genuine particles/kg-dry-weight value, so it must not be read
alongside the River water and Ocean water rows as a comparable risk finding.**

```{r spec3c-decomp-asa-legacy, include=FALSE}
# SPEC 3c: (iv) Hazard surface-area-slope alignment ONLY reverted to legacy
# (cumulative-as-differential); a.v/a.m, length alpha, and exposure all stay
# at their corrected values. This isolates a.sa alone, separate from the
# combined a.v+a.sa+a.m reversion already captured by risk_summary_legacy_river
# (Section 13.1) -- needed because Tissue Translocation/oxidative-stress
# alignment is surface-area-weighted, so it may be materially sensitive to
# a.sa even though it is not volume-weighted (unlike Food Dilution).
param_values_legacy_asa_river <- param_values |>
  dplyr::mutate(a.sa.freshwater = -cpsd_fit_area$a_cpsd, a.sa.freshwater.sd = cpsd_fit_area$se_a_cpsd)

set.seed(7008)
param_matrix_legacy_asa_river <- matrix_function(
  n = n_boot,
  params = param_values_legacy_asa_river,
  upper.tissue.truncation.limit = 500,
  x1M_set = 1,
  x2D_set = 5000
) |>
  mutate(R.ave.water.freshwater = sample(R.ave_vals, size = n(), replace = TRUE),
         H_W_ratio.freshwater   = sample(R.ave_vals, size = n(), replace = TRUE))

river_pssd_legacy_asa <- run_pssd_pipeline(
  tox_data     = tox_data,
  param_matrix = param_matrix_legacy_asa_river,
  environments = c("Freshwater"),
  cache_suffix = "river_legacy_asa",
  dose_unit    = "L",
  n_sim        = n_boot,
  num_cores    = parallel::detectCores() - 2,
  sim          = 30,
  cv_uf        = 0.5,
  rmore_method = "lognormal",
  seed         = 5008
)
haz_legacy_asa_river        <- build_haz_df(river_pssd_legacy_asa$pSSDs, "Freshwater")
set.seed(9309)
risk_draws_legacy_asa_river <- draw_rq_mc1d(haz_legacy_asa_river, eed_boot$q50, n_risk = n_risk)
risk_summary_legacy_asa_river <- summarize_rq(risk_draws_legacy_asa_river)
```

```{r spec3c-tissue-translocation-inline, include=FALSE}
tt_now       <- dplyr::filter(risk_summary, ERM == "Tissue Translocation", HCx == 5)
tt_legacy    <- dplyr::filter(risk_summary_legacy_alpha_river, ERM == "Tissue Translocation", HCx == 5)
tt_legacy_av <- dplyr::filter(risk_summary_legacy_river, ERM == "Tissue Translocation", HCx == 5)
tt_legacy_asa <- dplyr::filter(risk_summary_legacy_asa_river, ERM == "Tissue Translocation", HCx == 5)
fd_now       <- dplyr::filter(risk_summary, ERM == "Food Dilution", HCx == 5)
fd_legacy_av <- dplyr::filter(risk_summary_legacy_river, ERM == "Food Dilution", HCx == 5)
```

## 15.1 Revised uncertainty interpretation

The main unresolved methodological uncertainties are now: (1) µFTIR objective and the marginal 50–100 µm detection zone, and (2) transport-induced PSD structural uncertainty described by Hoffman et al. (2026). The latter can affect absolute concentrations through the CF exponent, and may also affect relative comparisons when surface/subsurface samples, fibers/fragments, or buoyant/settling polymers are mixed in a pooled single-power-law fit. The sensitivity analyses above therefore replace the older conclusion that no further correction was warranted. The calibrated interpretation is that the Food Dilution pathway remains the dominant ERM in this screening assessment, while magnitude estimates should be read together with the slope-uncertainty, depth-stratified, density/buoyancy, and water-sediment coherence diagnostics.

## 15.2 Modeling priorities

Hoffman et al. (2026) indicates that 3-D particle geometry and density inputs should be improved before investing effort in more complex settling-velocity equations. The current report follows that guardrail by adding polymer-resolved density and buoyancy flags, making δ and K explicit assumptions in the critical-size calculation, and retaining settling-based diagnostics as bias-level sensitivity checks rather than high-precision corrections. Future transport work should prioritize measured particle thickness, density, and shape-specific behavior; settling-equation refinements alone should not be expected to remove the dominant uncertainty.

## 15.3 SPEC 3b: Revised executive summary

```{r spec3b-exec-summary-inline, include=FALSE}
fd_river_hc5 <- dplyr::filter(risk_summary,       ERM == "Food Dilution", HCx == 5)
tt_river_hc5 <- dplyr::filter(risk_summary,       ERM == "Tissue Translocation", HCx == 5)
fd_sed_hc5   <- dplyr::filter(risk_summary_sed,   ERM == "Food Dilution", HCx == 5)
tt_sed_hc5   <- dplyr::filter(risk_summary_sed,   ERM == "Tissue Translocation", HCx == 5)
fd_legacy_av_hc5 <- dplyr::filter(risk_summary_legacy_river, ERM == "Food Dilution", HCx == 5)
fd_collapse_river <- fd_legacy_av_hc5$RQ_p50 / fd_river_hc5$RQ_p50
```

This section restates the executive summary with the corrected numbers now that every matrix's corrected and legacy sensitivity pipeline (Sections 5-14) has been computed, per SPEC 3b.

**(a) Corrected Food Dilution RQ, after SPEC 1b.** At this development-scale Monte Carlo budget (`r n_boot` parameter-matrix replicates, `r n_mc` slope draws), the corrected median Food Dilution HC5 RQ is `r round(fd_river_hc5$RQ_p50, 3)` for river water (P(RQ>1) = `r round(fd_river_hc5$P_exceed*100,1)`%) and `r round(rs_ocean_food_hc5$RQ_p50_med, 3)` for ocean water (median P(RQ>1) = `r round(rs_ocean_food_hc5$P_exceed_med*100,1)`%). **Sediment is intentionally omitted from this headline figure (SPEC 1d):** its nominal corrected Food Dilution HC5 RQ (`r round(fd_sed_hc5$RQ_p50, 3)`, P(RQ>1) = `r round(fd_sed_hc5$P_exceed*100,1)`%) is not a defensible risk estimate — Section 11.3.0/11.4.0 trace this to a placeholder exposure concentration (a per-liter water value reused as particles/kg) and a derived HC5 that fails the benthic-plausibility guard by roughly eleven orders of magnitude — so it is excluded from the risk conclusion rather than reported alongside the river and ocean values.

**(b) The prior (SPEC 1b-uncorrected) Food Dilution RQ was inflated by the volume-slope convention error.** Reverting only `a.v`/`a.sa`/`a.m` to the legacy cumulative-as-differential convention (Section 13.1), holding exposure and the length-slope alignment at their corrected values, the river-water Food Dilution HC5 median RQ becomes `r round(fd_legacy_av_hc5$RQ_p50, 3)` — a `r round(fd_collapse_river, 1)`-fold change relative to the corrected value of `r round(fd_river_hc5$RQ_p50, 3)` at this development-scale budget. This is the same mechanism, and the same direction of error, described in the SPEC 1b background (a mean-particle-volume sensitivity calculation there estimates a ~4-6 million-fold effect at a = 0.76 vs. 1.68); the smaller factor observed here reflects the small `n_boot`/`n_mc` development budget rather than a disagreement in mechanism, and should be re-checked at full production budget (Section 4 deliverables checklist) before this number is used externally. **No Food Dilution RQ figure in this report should be read as ~10^7 post-SPEC-1b** — that magnitude, if reproduced at production scale, describes the pre-SPEC-1b (legacy) error being corrected here, not the corrected result.

**(c) Tissue Translocation shift after both the length-slope and surface-area-slope fixes (revised, SPEC 3c).** Reverting only the hazard-side length-slope alignment to its legacy cumulative-as-differential form, the river-water Tissue Translocation HC5 P(RQ>1) is `r round(tt_legacy$P_exceed*100,1)`%, versus `r round(tt_now$P_exceed*100,1)`% under the corrected alignment (Section 14.1). This is a material driver, but so is the surface-area slope: reverting `a.v`/`a.sa`/`a.m` together gives `r round(tt_legacy_av$P_exceed*100,1)`%, and isolating `a.sa` alone gives `r round(tt_legacy_asa$P_exceed*100,1)`% — both far from the `r round(tt_now$P_exceed*100,1)`% corrected value, because Tissue Translocation/oxidative-stress alignment is surface-area-weighted and therefore directly sensitive to the `a.sa` correction, unlike its (correctly) minimal sensitivity to the volume slope alone. A prior version of this narrative incorrectly called the volume/area effect on Tissue Translocation "essentially unchanged"; that claim is retracted here (Section 14.1 has the corrected attribution and the full one-at-a-time decomposition table, now covering both ERMs).

**(d) Exposure as a single-slope-vs-piecewise bounding range (SPEC 2b).** The production single-slope correction factor and its piecewise (dual-slope) bounding alternative are compared per matrix in Section 13.3 (Tables: single-slope vs. piecewise CF/EED, and the resulting Food Dilution/Tissue Translocation HC5 RQ range). The single-slope CF remains the production default; the piecewise result is a labeled sensitivity bound quantifying structural (model-form) uncertainty in the unconstrained 1 µm-to-LOD sub-window, per the guardrails in the corrective-revision spec.

**(e) Sediment pathway excluded from the headline conclusion (SPEC 1d).** The sediment (beach sand) risk characterization in Section 11 is retained in this report as a methods/illustrative demonstration only. Its exposure concentration is not a genuine particles/kg-dry-weight value (Section 11.3.0), its hazard-side dose_unit = "kg" pathway was traced and found unit-consistent on its own terms with no discrete conversion bug identified (Section 11.4.0), and its sediment-specific ERM alignment slopes were independently verified correct and ruled out as the cause (Section 11.2, SPEC 1d-iv). The resulting sediment Food Dilution HC5 fails a rendered plausibility guard anchored on Redondo-Hasselerharm et al. (2023) by roughly eleven orders of magnitude. Until a genuine dry-weight sediment concentration is available, no sediment RQ in this report should be treated as a risk finding.

**(f) Sediment as a time-dependent, accumulating compartment (SPEC 1e).** Independent of the exposure-concentration problem in (e), Section 11.5 reframes sediment as an accumulating depositional sink in which deposited microplastics continue to fragment in place, so both bioaccessible exposure and hazard (HC5, via which benthic species become size-accessible) evolve over residence time ([Thuy-Dung, Groenenberg & Koelmans 2026](https://doi.org/10.1186/s43591-026-00210-8)). Any static sediment metric — including the illustrative Section 11.4 figures — is therefore a **lower-bound snapshot**, not an equilibrium value. Section 11.5.2 demonstrates this illustratively with a labeled, non-quantitative PSD-shift sensitivity showing the derived Food Dilution and Tissue Translocation HC5 falling as the sediment PSD is shifted progressively finer; Section 11.5.4 adds a most-sensitive-species screen (sediment, plus a river/ocean companion) since individual-species risk can precede a derivable community SSD signal. This is a framework/sensitivity addition — it does not change point (e): sediment remains excluded from the headline risk conclusion.

**Summary.** Food Dilution remains the risk-dominant ERM relative to Tissue Translocation for river and ocean water in this screening assessment, consistent with the qualitative conclusion of the prior revision; the sediment pathway is excluded from this conclusion pending real concentration data (point (e) above). The magnitude of the Food Dilution RQ, however, depends materially on which of the three convention fixes above is applied, and the decomposition in Section 14.1 is intended to make that dependency auditable rather than implicit. All figures in this section are development-scale (`r n_boot` replicates) and are flagged for human sign-off and a full-budget production re-run before external release, per the deliverables checklist.

## 15.4 SPEC 1e-iv: individual-species RCR — river/ocean companion screen

Section 11.5.4 added a most-sensitive-species screen for the sediment benthic dataset. This subsection completes SPEC 1e-iv's companion request for the water compartments where exposure *is* quantitative (river, ocean): the single most sensitive species per ERM, plus the individual-species risk characterization ratio RCR = EED / lowest-species EC, reported as an early-warning companion to the community-HC5 RQ already characterized in Sections 7/12. This is placed here, after Section 15.3, because it is the first point in document execution order at which every matrix's hazard (`haz`/`haz_ocean`) and EED (`eed_boot`/`eed_boot_ocean`) objects all exist together.
